article_text:
Wie jedes Jahr lädt Photo Vision Zumstein zum grossen Jahresfestival in Bern ein, mit dem grossen Marken- und Publikumstreffen in der Zeltstadt und den vielen Angeboten an Vorträgen, Workshops und Fotowalks. Und natürlich wie immer, viele Testgelegenheiten, Sonderaktionen und Schnäppchen.

Am Freitag 23. und Samstag, 24. Oktober 2026, findet wieder das grosse Fotofestival Wonderland von Zumstein in Bern statt. Auf dem Casinoplatz gibt es wiederum die legendäre Zeltstadt, und der frisch umgebaute Hauptsitz von Zumstein hat für Sie alle Türen offen.

Das Zumstein-Wonderland auf dem Casinoplatz

Wie alle Jahre wird auf dem Casinoplatz die grosse Zeltstadt aufgebaut, in der man nicht nur alle Markenspezialist/innen treffen und mit ihnen über Neuheiten und Technikfragen fachsimpeln kann, sondern der Ort ist auch die ideale Gelegenheit, um Gleichgesinnte und bekannte Persönlichkeiten zu treffen – kurz: ein Ort der Begegnungen und Vernetzungen.

Vorträge, Workshops und Photowalks

Einer der tragenden Pfeiler der Zumstein Wonderworld sind die Vorträge, Workshops und Photowalks. Hier wird in kurzen Sessions viel Praxiserfahrung der Referent/innen und professionelles Fachwissen vermittelt. Die Expert/innen geben ihre Erkenntnisse mit ihren Fotoausrüstungen auf ihren Expeditionen und praktische Ratschläge weiter, mit welchen Produkten sie besonders gute oder weniger glückliche Erfahrungen gemacht haben. Oder sie erzählen von spannenden Erlebnissen in Situationen unterwegs in freier Wildbahn oder entlegenen und wenig bekannten Regionen. Dann lernen Sie in Workshops worauf Sie für bestimmte Praxisaufgaben besonders achten müssen, oder Sie nehmen an einem der Fotowalks teil, auf denen Ihnen ein erfahrener Profi zeigt, was Sie in bestimmten Situationen mit Ihrer Ausrüstung besonders beachten müssen. Viele dieser Events sind aufgrund grosser Nachfrage bereits ausgebucht. Details dazu finden Sie unter diesem Link oder durch Mausklick auf die obenstehende Illustration.

Bei Photo Experience tauchen Sie ein in kreative Welten mit spannenden Fotosujets. Diverse Porträt-, Action- und Makromotive warten darauf, von Ihnen fotografiert zu werden: Entdecken, testen und erleben! Wo und wann? Maison & Casinoplatz, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Im Ferngucker-Bereich können Sie alle aktuellen Ferngläser, Spektive und Super-Teleobjektive verschiedener Marken vor Ort testen und sich von den Spezialisten beraten lassen. Wo und wann? Park Kochergasse 1, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

In der Zumirent Testbar kann man sich kostenlos sein Traum-Equipment aussuchen und vor Ort gleich testen. Dazu stehen die neuesten Kameras und Objektive aus dem Zumirent-Mietservice zur Verfügung, oder Sie können die gewünschten Zubehörteile gleich an Ihrer eigenen Ausrüstung praktisch erproben – all dies natürlich mit der professionellen Zumi-Beratung. Wann und Wo? Casinoplatz 8, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Ausstellungen und Markentreffen

Entdecken Sie die grosse Ausstellung an Kameras, Objektiven, Fernoptik und Zubehör. Nutzen Sie die Gelegenheit und tauschen Sie sich mit den Marken-Spezialist/innen direkt vor Ort aus. Wann und Wo? Casinoplatz, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Treffen Sie diese Markenspezialist/innen. Das ist die Gelegenheit, um die Produktespezialisten von Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, OM System, Leica, Zeiss, Rollei, Eizo, Nimax, Patona, Tamron, Insta360, Peak Design, Rode, Sigma, Hasselblad, DJI, Lowepro, Gitzo, Manfrotto, Novoflex, Vanguard, Voigtländer und vielen mehr persönlich zu treffen! Wann und Wo? Casinoplatz, Freitag Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Das Zwirbelrad-Gewinnspiel ist Ihre Chance, um einen tollen Preis zu gewinnen. Kommen Sie vorbei und drehen Sie daran. Vielleicht schlägt Ihre Glücksstunde … Wann und Wo? Casinoplatz, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Angebote und Promotionen

Im Coffee Corner im Maison können Sie sich jederzeit einen Coffee-to-go gönnen und sich gleich anschliessend von der Portrait Photo Experience inspirieren lassen. Wann und Wo? Maison, Freitag 10 bis 18 Uhr und Samstag 9 bis 17 Uhr

Im grossen Zumi-Ausverkauf gibt es Gebraucht- und Demogeräte aller Marken und Arten mit einem Rabatt bis 49 Prozent! Reinschauen lohnt sich auf alle Fälle! Hier geht es zum Ausverkauf .

Unter den Angeboten und Promotionen gibt es einzigartige Aktionen und Sonderpreise, die auf Sie warten. Darunter ganz besondere Schnäppchen von Canon, Fujifilm, Nikon, OM System, Panasonic, Sony, Sigma und Zeiss. Hier geht es zu den Sonderangeboten .

Alle Infos zum diesjährigen Photo Wonderland finden Sie unter www.foto-zumstein.ch

title_original: The ’60 Minutes’ Overhaul Was Said to be Driven by New Ideas — You Can’t Tell That from Watching
editorial_title_zh: 《60分钟》的大改版据称由新创意驱动——但你在观看时根本看不出来
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在巴里·韦斯和尼克·比尔顿上任之前，他们曾声称CBS广受欢迎的新闻节目正在走向过时。但在他们改版后的五集节目中，变化微乎其微，收视率也在下降。这究竟是怎么回事？

article_text:
When CBS News’ editor-in-chief Bari Weiss formally introduced executive producer Nick Bilton to steer “60 Minutes” into the future, the former writer on HBO’s “The Idol” sent a letter to his staff promising to “lead this show, not preserve it under glass.”

“I have a notebook full of ideas,” Bilton said. “Some are about the show itself. Some are about the next generation of correspondents. Some are about the strange fact that we produce one extraordinary hour for one night a week in a world that consumes content around the clock. I’m excited to share them.”

That excitement has not materialized onscreen. Not through five episodes, anyway.

For all the posturing around America’s No. 1 news program for 52 straight years needing a new direction, the latest season has shown scant evidence of what that new direction might be. The initial few months of Weiss and Hilton’s “ 60 Minutes ” look a lot like the last 50 years of the classic “60 Minutes.” Perhaps that uniformity stems from pushback faced by the new regime, internally and externally, which led to assurances from the co-founder of The Free Press and her chosen EP that the show would “stay exactly like it is for now.”

But as ratings plummet and controversies rise, one has to wonder when these grand ideas to save “60 Minutes” might manifest. If the series wasn’t an “ice cube that is melting” before, it’s certainly feeling the heat now . So what’s being done to cool things down?

Using Bilton’s own blueprint — his “notebook of ideas” — let’s start with the changes we can see so far, which aren’t that easy to spot. Do you think many returning viewers clocked the alterations to the opening stopwatch? The cropping is tighter. Less of the watch-face is shown. And instead of “60 Minutes” appearing in a white font on a red background, it’s now in a red font on a white background.

Another brazen shift comes in how stories are introduced: Before, the lead reporter sat in front of a rectangular digital backdrop that looked like an open book. Now, the lead reporter sits in front of a rectangular digital backdrop that looks like… nothing. It’s just a screen. Or maybe an e-reader?

To be fair, a segment in the third episode kicks off with an attention-grabbing switcheroo: An AI-generated version of contributor Jon Wertheim gives the intro, before the real reporter walks out to explain the reason behind the stunt. (Their story, titled “Who needs humans?,” covers AI’s impact on the workforce.) But anyone fooled by Wertheim’s CGI avatar either wasn’t watching closely or thought the host had suddenly grown mutant fingers and a developed a wobbly eye.

Wertheim’s report also featured walk-and-talk shots, a standard technique (on “60 Minutes” and elsewhere) used to liven up static interviews, but one that Bilton said he wanted to avoid this season. Elsewhere, Bilton revived a retired series staple: the hidden-camera interview, which was used in the premiere’s report on President Trump’s “Pardon Economy.”

A lot of the old and less of the new doesn’t add up to significant change, let alone a surefire way to avoid purported extinction. Perhaps Weiss and Bilton are drawing from Jack Donaghy’s idea notebook , and the grand plan is to “make it 1997 again through science and magic.” Or maybe it’s not about altering the package as much as who’s delivering it, like Bilton mentioned in his second “idea.”

New correspondent Ross Douthat earned some of the show’s rare positive headlines when he landed an interview with Patrick Clancy . But where others may have heard pensive, sensitive questions fashioned for a man who’s been put through the ringer, online and off, I saw a reporter without the requisite patience and attentiveness to push a much-hyped interview beyond expectations. While sitting in a playground built as memorial for his dead children, Clancy chokes up recalling recurring dreams of his ex-wife. Douthat, meanwhile, can be seen tapping his leg and smiling.

Active listening is a skill, and Douthat rarely feels present. He’s awkward and terse, stilted and inexpressive. If his smile is meant to be reassuring, it comes off as clumsy, and the tapping is just plain rude.

No matter how you read Douthat’s comportment (his garbled narration, slouched posture, and rumpled suit don’t exactly scream “professional”), there’s no reason to assume he’s why “60 Minutes” — once the most respected name in news — booked a sought-after subject like Clancy, just as there’s no reason to believe his addition to the team is the trollish stewardship needed to court younger viewers or retain older ones. (There is reason to believe handing him a position on “60 Minutes” helped transfer his popular conservative print column from The New York Times to the Weiss-run Free Press — the reason being, that’s exactly what happened .)

As for the other new contributors, only one has issued a report: Ariel Levy, whose profile on Sacha Baron Cohen capped the latest episode. In five weeks, Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni, and Trevor Phillips have only appeared during “The Last Minute,” the closing segment that typically updates old stories or teases new ones. Their seconds-long spiels have touched on topical news instead, providing brief summaries of subjects like the protests in Europe and the war in Ukraine, as if long-form journalism is incomplete without a quick nod to the daily headlines.

That just leaves Bilton’s last idea: the “strange fact” that “60 Minutes” only airs “one night a week in a world that consumes content around the clock.” What he means by this is vague, even compared to his other unspecified ideas, which makes it even more difficult to imagine how it might be realized.

No spinoffs or extensions of “60 Minutes” have been announced, and its social media pages are comparable to previous years. YouTube features individual segments, full episodes, and archival content. TikTok hosts similar footage, albeit clipped for vertical video and treated with title cards. X is filled with a handful of videos every day, just as it was before Bilton’s hiring. (Based on a cursory scroll, previous social posts led with popular contributors like Anderson Cooper, whereas current stories — now without those popular contributors — tend to lead with the subjects.)

Perhaps pioneering new media strategies and must-see additional programming are still on the way, but for now, Bilton’s notebook of ideas has yet to yield appreciable results. The ratings, spun positively, are dependent on a good NFL lead-in .

Seen plainly, they’re setting record lows . Meanwhile, “60 Minutes” still looks like “60 Minutes”: No changes in these first five episodes could be expected to entice fresh viewers to tune in or convince alienated viewers to reconsider.

So, as a CBS senior staffer put it , “Why did you have to fire everyone to get a vaguely passable facsimile” of the original show?

Enter the 800-pound gorilla in any article about a Weiss-run “60 Minutes,” aka what really worries longtime viewers, true-blue journalists, and any honest supporter of the First Amendment: Rather than superficial changes to how the newsroom’s stories are shared, will there be an ideological shift in how those stories are reported — or what stories are reported at all?

Weiss, who’s nearly as proud of her conservatism as she is of her Zionism , validated those fears from the jump. The David Ellison -appointee (who has a fan in Donald Trump) reportedly introduced herself to “60 Minutes” producers by asking, “Why does the country think you’re biased?” Then she spiked a story critical of the Trump administration and, six months later, fired the venerated contributor Scott Pelley after he accused her of “murdering” the program. Her tenure is only possible because Ellison acquired CBS’ parent company, Paramount, which, in turn, only seemed possible because the network settled a controversial lawsuit against “60 Minutes” brought on by President Trump.

And yet “60 Minutes” — the country’s highest-rated news program for five decades — is what Americans consider biased?

Perhaps there’s an argument for bias now, when the only framing of the president’s “deeply unpopular” war in Iran is under the flattering guise of saving a soldier from behind enemy lines (Episode 1, “Shot Down Over Iran”). Or when Douthat helped Republican Senator Thom Tillis sell copies of his book by praising him for voting along party lines while “talking and maneuvering like a maverick” (Episode 3, “The Thom Tillis Tightrope”). Or when the best, most substantial story of the season (Episode 4, “Lost Sheep”) led to reports of interference that pushed Lesley Stahl to “the brink of quitting.”

These are the only biases, the only changes, viewers can see. Maybe more are coming. Or maybe the steady, unobtrusive creep of conservatism has been the idea all along.
excerpt_original: Prior to their tenure, Bari Weiss and Nick Bilton claimed CBS's popular news program was becoming obsolete. But through five episodes of their revamped version, changes are negligible and ratings are down. What gives?

article_text:
Three movies later, Jane Levy is teasing Evil Dead fans about a potential return for her character Mia Allen after she survived the bloody events of the 2013 reboot.

During a post-screening Q&A for the Fede Álvarez-written/directed horror film, which was hosted by Contra Celluloid, the actress fueled recent rumors that she will reprise her character for the 2028 prequel Evil Dead Wrath or a future installment in the Sam Raimi franchise.

“I have a question. Do you guys think Mia should come back to Evil Dead ?” she asked in a video from the Q&A, igniting applause from the audience. “OK cool, I was just checking. That’s all.”

article_text:
The 1990s were a very different time — especially in Silver Lake, California — once a fertile neighborhood of artists and musicians and now a pricey hot spot. Three decades ago, the indie music scene was flourishing with homegrown acts like Beck and Rilo Kiley, based around clubs like Spaceland and the Garage.

And for more than two heady years, music lovers within a mile or two of the Sunset Junction area could groove to the wildly eclectic sounds of KBLT, a pirate radio station that operated from 1995 to 1998.

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo's 'Bad Fairies' Adds Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to Voice Cast

Cynthia Erivo Called Sunny Hostin to Explain Why 'The View' Host's Comments on Cornell 7 Case Sparked Backlash: 'Lead With Empathy' and Not the Law

The mystique of the scrappy station is told in the new documentary “ 40 Watts From Nowhere ,” a fond look back at the Silver Lake music scene and the bands and personalities that came through KBLT. The doc premiered at Slamdance in February and, thanks to Jack Black stepping in as executive producer, it got the attention of Amazon Prime, where begins streaming Tuesday.

KBLT was the brainchild of Sue Carpenter, a journalist and music lover who learned about a “legal bubble” that enabled people to start low-power radio stations without prohibitively expensive FCC licenses. Carpenter learned how to put such a station together from Berkeley, California pirate radio guru Stephen Dunifer, got help building a transmitter, and started her first radio project, KPBJ, in her San Francisco apartment. After moving to L.A., Carpenter (using a pseudonym) selected another food-themed acronym and started making connections to line up DJs.

Opening with shots of Silver Lake’s iconic Walking Man and Happy Foot Sad Foot sign, the documentary is packed with vintage footage of the station and its DJs, from the Red Hot Chili Peppers to DJs Mike Watt of the Minutemen, Don Bolles of the Germs and Keith Morris of the Circle Jerks. Also featured are scenes of mid-90s Silver Lake and contemporary interviews with Tom Morello and others who got started around the time.

“What is the answer to corporate ownership of the media?” Morello asks in the film. “Get rid of it. Let’s start over.”

Where did all this nostalgic footage come from? Years after the station shut down, Carpenter was amazed to find out that one of the station’s DJs had boxes of videos of the station in a box in his garage.

“I would never have made this documentary if this video hadn’t existed,” says Carpenter. “Even though there was a sit-down interview with me, and I was shooting some of this video, I have no recollection of ever having done that.” Robert Sullivan, known as Sully from the band Possum Dixon, was shooting the footage for a documentary he never made. After Carpenter wrote a book about KBLT, “Sully just sort of sort of piped up,” says Carpenter. He said, “You know, I have all these videos. They’re just in a box in my garage. I’m about to throw them out. Do you want them?

“I went through the video and was shocked that he pretty much had the whole arc of the story, and that made me feel like I could make a documentary out of it,” she says.

Carpenter had no special background in radio or music before deciding to start the station. “I just wanted to do it,” she says. “Naïveté has been my superpower, and not knowing what it takes — if I had known, I would not have done it,” she says. “You get to a certain point, and there’s another hurdle, and you just have to cross it, and then you get on air, and then it just feels magical.”

After the transmitter was up and running, a 24/7 schedule came together with help from Brandon Jay, the drummer of Silver Lake’s Lutefisk, who became a co-producer on “40 Watts.” The station didn’t just play indie rock — Carpenter’s show was dedicated to French pop, while other DJs spun the blues, jazz, prog rock, punk, funk and techno.

“You didn’t know who would be playing what, and if you turned it on the radio, you didn’t know what you would be hearing, or who would be talking,” says “40 Watts” music supervisor Mara Kuge

It was a time when hearing something out of the mainstream on the radio could pretty much blow your mind, Kuge recalls.

“I don’t even know if people understand the wow factor of hearing something like that back then and knowing, ‘OK, there’s somebody else who listens to the same pretty obscure at the time music that I do, and who is this person, and how can I find it?’” Kuge says.

“It was basically Sue and her cat living in a one-bedroom apartment in Silver Lake with a parade of people she didn’t know, including strange men,” Kuge explains. Carpenter attributes her open-door policy to being a “curious person” with “no boundaries,” though it did result in cleaning up a lot of beer bottles. “It’s not like everyone was a total fucking slob, but there were enough who were when you get that many people together,” she remembers.

The station’s mystique grew when some of the hottest bands of the time dropped by to play live sets, including the Red Hot Chili Peppers, who squeezed into the hallway to play.

The doc’s soundtrack includes dozens of bands the station frequently played, including Bikini Kill, Rage Against the Machine, Elliott Smith, Mudhoney, and Fugazi, who rarely license their music.

Less than three years later, it all came crashing down when Berkeley’s Dunifer lost his case and FCC officials moved quickly to shut down KBLT.

Carpenter, who went on to become a motorcycle columnist for the L.A. Times and then a radio and TV journalist, is surprised there hasn’t been more content about the distinctive sounds of that time.

“Honestly, I thought that people would have given it more documentation by now,” she says. “Our scene was really, really creative and colorful.”

Carpenter says today’s Silver Lake, with its corporate boutiques and private-equity restaurants, feels foreign to her. “I feel like I don’t relate to the neighborhood anymore, because it’s become so commercial. The mom-and-popness of it, the heart of it, doesn’t feel like it’s there anymore.”

As DJ and Thelonious Monster musician Bob Forrest says in the doc, “Silver Lake was magical. KBLT was this beautiful cherry on top of this beautiful time in Los Angeles.”

article_text:
Amelia Dimoldenberg ‘s “ Chicken Shop Date ” is coming to the big screen.

To celebrate its final series after 12 years, Dimoldenberg is holding a one-night-only event on Nov. 24 at cinemas in the U.K., Ireland and Paris in collaboration with YouTube’s Cine Club. All six episodes of the final series — which so far includes interviews with Oasis’ Noel Gallagher, Role Model and Jorja Smith — will be screened together in one “cinematic experience,” per a press release, featuring exclusive new material. The screening will culminate with the final unreleased episode, giving fans a chance to see it before it drops on YouTube Nov. 27.

Related Stories

'Fourth Wing' TV Series Casts Esther McGregor and Emilio Sakraya as Violet Sorrengail and Xaden Riorson

'Carrie' Renewed for Season 2 at Amazon

The “Chicken Shop Date” film will also “offer a personal look behind the series, exploring Amelia’s relationship with the show and her decision to bring it to an end,” the release states. “Moving between comedy, nostalgia and candid reflection, the film is both a celebration of everything ‘Chicken Shop Date’ has become and a fitting farewell to one of the internet’s most recognizable formats.”

Theaters screening the final “Chicken Shop Date” series on Nov. 24 include Duke of York’s Picturehouse in Brighton; Picturehouse Central and Curzon Soho in London; mk2 Bibliothèque in Paris; Vue Manchester Printworks; Vue Edinburgh Omni Centre; Vue Bristol Cribbs Causeway; Vue Birmingham Star City; Vue Dublin Liffey Valley; and Vue London Westfield.

The public screenings will be preceded by invite-only premieres in London on Nov. 16 and New York City on Nov. 17, where Dimoldenberg will also participate in Q&As.

Dimoldenberg revealed that “Chicken Shop Date” would be coming to an end last month, writing in a social media post: “I never thought I’d stop ‘Chicken Shop Date,’ I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one.”

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Obsession ‘s Megan Lawless and three-time Emmy nominee Lili Taylor ( Outer Range ) are among new additions to PRƎPPY , the true-crime flick from STX Entertainment and Aggregate Films that we announced in September.

Others include Gideon Adlon ( Euphoria ), Jaeden Martell ( It ), James Wilkie Broderick ( Lady in the Lake ), Jaya Harper ( Roommates ), Jahi Winston ( Charm City Kings ), and Alex Consani ( American Horror Story ).

The film, directed by Janicza Bravo, is now in production in Manhattan. Kit Connor, Diana Silvers, and Talia Ryder lead the cast, as we previously reported.

Related Stories

Talia Ryder, Elizabeth Marvel & Bill Camp Join STX & Aggregate's True-Crime Thriller 'PRƎPPY'

'Obsession' Star Megan Lawless Boards Indie Romantic Comedy 'Crushed'

Based on an original screenplay by David Levine and Rose Lichter-Marck, PRƎPPY explores the summer of 1986 leading to the murder of recent high school graduate Jennifer Levin at the hands of Robert Chambers, a former Manhattan private-school student, in New York’s Central Park. The shocking crime — in which Chambers was dubbed the “Preppy Killer” — captivated a generation and put privilege, class and sex on trial.

Watch on Deadline

Jason Bateman, Michael Costigan and John Buderwitz are producing for Aggregate, alongside Peter Coleman and Paula Manzanedo for STX, and Bravo. Elizabeth Marvel and Bill Camp also star.

Fresh off a breakout role in Curry Barker’s horror hit Obsession , Lawless’ earlier credits included The Girl from Plainville , The Hate U Give , and Table 19 . She is repped by 42 Management & Production, Alexander White Agency, and Yorn Levine.

Taylor’s recent projects include Daredevil: Born Again and The Conjuring: Last Rites . She plays Mags Flanagan in The Hunger Games: Sunshine on the Reaping , out November 20, and recently wrapped a role opposite Billie Eilish in Sarah Polley’s The Bell Jar . She is repped by Independent Artist Group, Untitled, and Schreck Rose Dapello.

Adlon is repped by UTA, Anonymous Content, and McKuin Frankel Whitehead; Martell by CAA, Emily Cho Talent Management, and Jackoway Austen; Broderick by Entertainment 360 and Innovative Artists; Harper by CAA and Untitled; Winston by WME and attorney Ryan LeVine; and Consani by Underscore Talent and IMG.

title_original: Crítica | Ponto Sem Retorno (2026): quando o fim do mundo não passa de uma paisagem
editorial_title_zh: 影评 | 《Ponto Sem Retorno》（2026年）：当世界末日不过是一处风景
editorial_excerpt_zh: 雷德利·斯科特在废墟之中找到了美丽的影像，却没有找到能赋予后末日布景以深度的角色或想法。本文《 影评 | 《Ponto Sem Retorno》（2026年）：当世界末日不过是一处风景》首先发布于 Cinema com Rapadura 。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "雷德利·斯科特在废墟之中找到了美丽的影像，却没有找到能赋予后末日布景以深度的角色或想法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在雷德利·斯科特的镜头前，《Ponto Sem Retorno》中的整个世界都已毁灭，但其中似乎很少有东西能存在于导演的取景框之外。雅各布·埃洛迪饰演Hig，一名带着狗穿梭于这片布景中的幸存者。找到其他人的可能性将他从抑郁的漩涡中拉了出来，并开启了一段汇聚该类型常见元素的旅程，例如孤立的社区、匮乏的资源、暴力团伙和不稳定的联盟。然而，作品并未在这些惯例中找到任何独特的视角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯科特以相当沉思的方式开场，意在衡量主角的孤独感并传达崩溃的范围。只是电影花了很长时间才让所有这些空间真正变成一个故事。对于幸存者是如何重新组织他们的生活，或者对于在社会崩塌后生活多年的实际后果，没有任何好奇心。所有的废墟最终构成了一种对后末日意象的有限模仿，这种意象已经在该类型的许多其他作品中屡见不鲜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所有这些肤浅性也同样限制了角色。埃洛迪在沉默的时刻表现得不错，并与狗建立了一种情感联系，但他的主角仅由忧郁来定义，而这并未被用于深化任何其他特征或情感。甚至他那过度保持完好的外表也削弱了本应伴随那种存在的沧桑感。乔什·布兰农（Josh Brolin）作为经验丰富且具有保护欲的幸存者很有存在感，尽管剧本几乎没有做任何事情来让他脱离这种原型。玛格丽特·库利、盖·皮尔斯、本尼迪克特·王和艾莉森·珍妮都是敬业的伟大演员，但他们得到的空间比其存在感所暗示的要少。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管时长不到两小时，这部电影看起来却更长。许多镜头，尤其是航拍镜头，看起来很美，但似乎只是为了强化Hig作为飞行员的职业。当斯科特打破最初的惯性、围绕威胁组织空间并最终接近动作戏时，这部长片展现出了残存的活力。然而，这位电影制作人甚至无法利用一个有趣的设定，在没有风险的情况下结束冲突，并且在充分挖掘其可能性之前就收场了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演表现敌对群体的方式也是有问题的。我们没有看到崩溃后可能出现的不同组织形式，这就浪费了一个让社会宇宙变得更加复杂的机会。电影将他们简化为由尖叫和彩绘所定义的攻击性部落——几乎是对通常与美洲原住民相关的陈旧“野蛮”图像学的重新演绎。当主角们保持着可辨认的行为和服装时，他们的对手却被去人性化，以便道德划分能够瞬间呈现。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着长片走向结局，一种叙事的不和谐感变得分外明显。主要角色抵达了一个改造成社区的机场，这又是一个展示社会可能正试图如何重建的机会。但这一段落引入了一种极其讽刺的基调，感觉像是属于另一部电影。艾莉森·珍妮拥抱了古怪，并且似乎在享受这个角色，然而所有这些外放的表演、加上该地方复古的组织形式以及突如其来的幽默，与先前的严肃性发生了冲突，这仅仅凸显了缺乏统一性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种宏大感与内容之间的距离定义了《Ponto Sem Retorno》。在最后的部分，旅程正是在本该找到回报的时候开始失去意义，它拉长了一个实际上已经暴露出它所能提供的全部内容——而且并不多——的故事。到处都是满目疮痍的世界的宽广且同质的影像；唯独缺少能够让这个世界显得真正迷失的人和想法。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Ridley Scott encontra belas imagens entre as ruínas, mas não personagens ou ideias capazes de dar profundidade ao cenário pós-apocalíptico.

O mundo inteiro de “ Ponto Sem Retorno ” está destruído diante da câmera de Ridley Scott, mas pouco dele parece existir além do enquadramento do diretor. Jacob Elordi interpreta Hig, um sobrevivente que atravessa esse cenário acompanhado de seu cachorro. A possibilidade de encontrar outras pessoas o retira de uma espiral depressiva e dá início a uma jornada que reúne elementos típicos do gênero, como comunidades isoladas, recursos escassos, grupos violentos e alianças instáveis. Contudo, a obra não encontra qualquer perspectiva particular nessas convenções.

Scott inicia de forma bastante contemplativa com a intenção de dimensionar a solidão do protagonista e comunicar a extensão do colapso. Só que o filme demora a fazer com que todo esse espaço vire uma história de fato. Não existe qualquer curiosidade sobre como os sobreviventes reorganizaram suas vidas ou sobre as consequências práticas de anos vivendo depois da queda da sociedade. Todas as ruínas acabam compondo uma emulação limitada do imaginário pós-apocalíptico já visto em tantas outras produções do gênero.

Toda essa superficialidade é um limitador também para os personagens. Elordi funciona nos momentos de silêncio e estabelece uma relação afetiva com o cachorro, mas seu protagonista é definido unicamente pela melancolia, sem que isso seja utilizado para aprofundar qualquer outra característica ou sentimento. Até sua aparência excessivamente preservada enfraquece a sensação de desgaste que deveria acompanhar aquela existência. Josh Brolin tem presença como o sobrevivente experiente e protetor, embora o roteiro pouco faça para afastá-lo desse arquétipo. Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce, Benedict Wong e Allison Janney são grandes nomes que se dedicam, mas recebem menos espaço do que suas presenças poderiam sugerir.

Apesar de ter menos de duas horas, o filme aparenta durar ainda mais. Muitas sequências, principalmente as tomadas aéreas, são bonitas de se ver, mas parecem existir apenas para reforçar o ofício de piloto de Hig. O longa mostra resquícios de energia quando Scott rompe a inércia inicial, organiza o espaço em torno das ameaças e finalmente se aproxima da ação. Acontece que o cineasta não consegue aproveitar nem mesmo uma ambientação interessante, encerrando o conflito sem riscos e antes de explorar plenamente suas possibilidades.

Também é problemática a maneira como os grupos hostis são representados pelo diretor. Não vemos diferentes formas de organização que poderiam surgir após o colapso, desperdiçando uma oportunidade de tornar o universo socialmente mais complexo. O filme os reduz a hordas agressivas, definidas por gritos e pinturas corporais — quase uma releitura de uma iconografia antiquada de “selvageria” comumente associada a nativos americanos. Enquanto os protagonistas mantêm comportamentos e roupas reconhecíveis, seus adversários são desumanizados para que a divisão moral permaneça imediata.

À medida que o longa se encaminha para o desfecho, uma desarmonia narrativa fica bastante exposta. Os personagens principais chegam a um aeroporto convertido em uma comunidade, em mais uma oportunidade de mostrar como a sociedade poderia estar tentando se reconstruir. Mas a sequência introduz um registro de tom tão satírico que parece pertencer a outro filme. Allison Janney abraça a excentricidade e parece se divertir com o papel, porém toda essa atuação expansiva, junto com a organização retrô do lugar e o humor repentino, entra em choque com a sobriedade anterior, apenas evidenciando a falta de unidade.

Essa distância entre dimensão e conteúdo define “Ponto Sem Retorno”. No trecho final, a jornada começa a perder propósito justamente quando deveria encontrar sua recompensa, prolongando uma história que já revelou praticamente tudo o que tinha a oferecer — e não era muito. Sobram imagens amplas e genéricas de um mundo devastado; faltam pessoas e ideias capazes de fazer esse mundo parecer perdido de verdade.

title_original: Sod’s law: what can two turf swaps 40 years apart tell us about Britain’s biodiversity crisis?
editorial_title_zh: 墨菲定律：相隔40年的两次草皮对调向我们揭示了英国的生物多样性危机吗？
editorial_excerpt_zh: 1983年，大卫·纳什（David Nash）挖出肯辛顿花园的一段草皮，并将其与威尔士的草地进行了对调。四十年后，迈克·佩里（Mike Perry）的反向对调揭示出城市与乡村自然命运的惊人逆转 1983年，一辆敞篷卡车在……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "1983年，一辆敞篷卡车在肯辛顿花园卸下了一批不寻常的货物：83块从威尔士费斯特尼奥格（Ffestiniog）山谷中林木茂盛的山坡地卡埃恩伊科德（Cae’n y Coed）切割下来的草皮。为了腾出空间放置这些威尔士草皮，伦敦西部蛇形画廊（Serpentine Gallery）旁边的公园里被挖出了一个直径8米呈环状的草皮，随后这些伦敦草皮被货车运往北威尔士。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大卫·纳什（David Nash）的一件具有雕塑反叛精神的作品《草皮对调》（Sod Swap）就这样拉开了序幕，它拥有意想不到且气势恢宏的后续生命。40多年后，摄影艺术家迈克·佩里（Mike Perry）以《反向草皮对调》（Reverse Sod Swap）重现了这件作品，在伦敦东部哈克尼（Hackney）的斯普林菲尔德公园（Springfield Park）与彭布罗克郡（Pembrokeshire）的牧场之间对调了等量的草皮，其结果却截然不同。在物种灭绝与气候危机频发的时代，这两件双生作品被赋予了新的现实意义，这场草皮对调也成了一本新书的主题。", "links": "paragraph", "text": "当纳什的那小块威尔士草皮适应汉普斯特德荒野时，这位艺术家在卡埃恩伊科德一丝不苟地给伦敦草皮浇水，甚至买了一台二手割草机，以便能让它保持习惯的状况。最初的计划是把它送回肯辛顿花园，但纳什说艺术委员会（Arts Council）告诉他项目资金已经用完，无法承担将其运回的费用。《草皮对调》成了永久性的装置。", "translated": true}, "逆向移植结束后，植物学家对移植的草皮进行了调查，惊奇地发现其结果与纳什1983年的交换恰好相反。取自斯普林菲尔德公园的草皮总共包含39种物种，而威尼斯（原文如此，指威尔士）牧羊场取来的草皮仅包含4种物种。因此，历经40年，这两件作品鲜明地展现了乡村生物多样性的丧失——这种丧失往往被英国乡村表面上不变的特征所掩饰，那些由树篱、田野和树林交织成的拼图掩盖了危机。但《逆向草皮交换》同时也揭示了伦敦更具希望的趋势，从在公园里打造野花区到建设新型可持续城市排水区，城市野化努力让物种得以复苏。", "paragraph", "text": "纳什为他的《草皮交换》能够历久弥新及其承载的生态讯息深感触动。“迈克所做的一切是一个惊人的加分项，”他说。“我的《草皮交换》凸显了伦敦植物物种的匮乏，尽管这并非我的主要意图。《逆向草皮交换》在环保层面上更具现实意义，因为它凸显了乡村土地的贫瘠。我们艺术家把作品呈现出来，希望人们能看到并从中领悟——受到启发或是将其作为自身环保意识的一部分。”", article_text:
I n 1983, an open-topped truck unloaded an unusual cargo in Kensington Gardens: 83 hunks of turf cut from Cae’n y Coed, a wooded hillside in the Ffestiniog valley. The ring of turf measuring eight metres in diameter that was removed from the park beside the Serpentine Gallery in west London to make space for the Welsh sods was then trucked from London to north Wales.

So began Sod Swap, a piece of sculptural defiance by David Nash , which has had an unexpected and epic afterlife. More than 40 years later, photographic artist Mike Perry restaged the work as Reverse Sod Swap , exchanging exactly the same amount of turf between Springfield Park in Hackney, east London, and pastureland in Pembrokeshire, with strikingly different results. With twin works acquiring new relevance in a time of extinction and climate crises, the sod swapping is now the subject of a new book.

It all began, says Nash, who is 80 and still working with wood and trees, with his own “bloody-mindedness”. He was invited to contribute to a new Serpentine gallery show of British sculpture. He submitted an idea of some wood sculptures for an indoor gallery because he felt too many outdoor sculptures were “like UFOs, they came and they went”, as he puts it. “But the gallery said: ‘Oh, David, you’re an outside artist, so we’d like you to participate in the outdoor space.”

Nash, who made his very outdoorsy Ash Dome and Wooden Boulder a few years before, bristled. He’d actually created an outdoor piece for a Serpentine show when he was a postgrad student at Chelsea Art School in 1970. When he tried to secure it in the ground he was told he couldn’t touch the Kensington Gardens turf because it belonged to the queen.

So this time, he plotted to rough up the manicured London park’s immaculate lawns by installing a ring of wild grassland from north Wales while also challenging definitions of “sculpture”. There was a lot of “bright red metal” around in the early 80s, says Nash wryly. “I wanted to create something that didn’t need to be cleaned.”

Sod Swap, he says, was a declaration of his identity. “I was very keen that what I put in had a sense of where it came from, which was where I was, which was north Wales.” When he realised he would have to dig up a load of Kensington turf, he decided to take that back to Wales. “That became the swap, and I liked the connotation of being a sod. It was nothing to do with the environment, really, but it turned out to be.”

Nash was anticipating a reaction and he got one. After several worried meetings about the dig, and head-scratching from council officials about the risk of “invasive” Welsh plants contaminating Kensington Gardens, Sod Swap went ahead. “He’s very subversive, David,” says Perry . “He doesn’t look it, but he is. The Serpentine expected him to bring in a big wooden sculpture. And he said: ‘No, I’m going to cut up your lawn.’ He wanted to show who he is as a person but also what sculpture could be – it doesn’t have to be a solid object on a plinth. It can be an ephemeral piece of organic material.”

In 2023, when Perry started a rewilding and art project on 4.9 hectares (12 acres) of farmland in west Wales, he wondered if he might revisit Nash’s concept, four decades on. Slightly nervously, he contacted Nash, and was relieved when the sculptor gave an enthusiastic “yes”. A week later, Perry drove over to north Wales, where Nash took him to see the site of the Kensington Garden sods. Amazingly, 40 years on, they could still detect a faint circle in mossy grass now punctuated by mature trees.

The Welsh turf hadn’t lasted so long in London. After the show ended, the gallery planned to simply to remove the turf but, thankfully for Nash, the “archangels of art outside”, Sue Clifford and Angela King, stepped in. The two co-founders of environmental arts charity Common Ground hurriedly found another unlikely London home for Nash’s Welsh sods: in the lawns of Kenwood House on Hampstead Heath.

Clifford and King also had the bright idea of convening ecologists to count the species in each turf circle. The Welsh sods held 28 different species, including grasses, wildflowers, brambles and even nettles, while the manicured sods cut from Kensington Gardens were made up of a meagre three different species of grass. Suddenly, Nash’s little challenge to the art world held an ecological message, highlighting the biodiversity to be found in rural meadowlands and the sterile quality of urban parks.

While Nash’s little piece of Wales acclimatised to Hampstead Heath, the artist conscientiously watered the London turf at Cae’ny Coed, even buying a secondhand mower so he could keep it in the condition to which it was accustomed. The original plan was to return it to Kensington Gardens, but Nash says the Arts Council told him they had run out of project money and couldn’t afford to transport it back. Sod Swap became permanent.

Eventually, after 10 years at Kenwood House, English Heritage removed the Welsh sods. “The London turf stayed in Wales,” remembers Nash. “Chestnut trees I planted grew and grew and shaded the turf, and moss came in. There were daisies from London which came up for about five years but then disappeared. I kept up mowing it as if it was in London for 20 years until it was virtually all moss and then I thought I would let it go.” Over the years, artists, curators and students made a pilgrimage to visit it.

Reverse Sod Swap was “a kind of biographical piece for me,” says Perry. He lived in London for 20 years before moving to an old farm by the sea in north Pembrokeshire. “My parents retired down here so I’ve always been going between east London and west Wales,” he says. The landscape and seascape of the Pembrokeshire Coast national park still looks gorgeous but “it’s a very melancholy thing walking down to the sea because there’s nothing in the hedges. They’re stripped right back and the grass is just mown 24/7 by so many sheep. The chair of the RSPB [Royal Society for the Protection of Birds] said national parks are where wildlife goes to die.”

Perry had hoped Reverse Sod Swap would be an ecological statement, but he couldn’t have anticipated just how much of a statement it would make. In Wales, he took the turf from pasture still heavily grazed by sheep belonging to a tenant farmer. At the London end, he was given “a really poor” plot in Springfield Park with “bad bits of soil from everywhere and a little bit of grass out of all sorts of rough material. But I quite liked it because there were giant burdocks and ‘weeds’ and thistles. I liked that mix.”

Perry’s first challenge was to replicate the dimensions. Nash couldn’t remember the exact size of his 1983 turf circles but Perry dug out the old catalogue statement, which noted that there were 83 sods measuring 90x30cm (35x12in) in size. He then followed Nash’s idea of making little wooden “stretchers” to carry each sod from the ground to the waiting lorry. On the journey to Wales, they twice stopped at motorway services to water the precious sods.

In the two-and-a-half years since Reverse Sod Swap, Perry has been surprised by how the project has continued to transfix him. “David put his hand on my shoulder and looked me in the eye and said: ‘Mike, when you make work outside, things happen.’ I didn’t really know what he meant. But what’s amazing is that the work is living and changing all the time – it keeps giving me new images and new findings.”

After the reverse transplant, botanists surveyed the transplanted turfs and, strikingly, found the reverse of Nash’s 1983 swap. The turf taken from Springfield Park contained 39 species in total, whereas the Welsh sheep-grazed turf contained just four species. And so, across four decades, the two works starkly illustrate the loss of rural biodiversity – a loss often disguised by the superficially unchanging character of the British landscape, with its patchwork of hedges, fields and woods. But Reverse Sod Swap also reveals a more hopeful trend in London, where species have been revived by urban rewilding efforts, from creating wildflower areas in parks to building new sustainable urban drainage areas.

Perry is encouraged by what he sees when he returns to London and walks down the Grand Union canal. “It feels like there’s butterflies, there’s rough stuff. It’s not scientific because there are obviously areas in Wales that can’t be farmed and there’s amazing biodiversity, but I was just really trying to make a point through art.”

Nash is touched by the longevity of his Sod Swap, and the ecological message it has taken on. “What Mike has done is an amazing bonus,” he says. “My Sod Swap highlighted the paucity of plant species in London, not that that was my main intention. Reverse Sod Swap is much more pertinent environmentally because it’s highlighting the paucity of rural land. We artists put work out there and hope people will see it and make something of it – be stimulated or take it on as part of their awareness.”

Reverse Sod Swap by Mike Perry and David Nash is published by Little Toller on 16 October (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

article_text:
Films and events

Dare

Rose

Sandra Hüller gives an award-winning performance as a 17th-century female soldier who disguises herself as a man to gain acceptance in a brutal farming community.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Markus Schleinzer

Screenwriters Markus Schleinzer, Alexander Brom

With Sandra Hüller, Caro Braun, Marisa Growaldt

Austria-Germany 2026. 94min

Courtesy of MUBI

Language German With English subtitles

Access information

Tuesday 13 October 18:00

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Thursday 15 October 15:10

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

In the aftermath of the ferocious Thirty Years’ War, a scarred female soldier dangerously inveigles her way into a strict rural community by posing as a man with an inheritance. Seemingly dispassionate in its watchful, austere monochrome, yet quietly devastating in its unflinching look at gender-based prejudice and intolerance, Markus Schleinzer’s masterful film is another triumph for Hüller.

Leigh Singer

With thanks to the Austrian Cultural Forum London.

Content advice

Contains scenes of sexual violence.

Contains transphobic attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Fatherland

In a masterclass of control and precision, Paweł Pawlikowski explores the fragmented soul of postwar Germany through a father-daughter road trip dominated by personal ghosts.

Woman Unknown

In May el-Toukhy’s powerful third feature, Marie, a survivor with secrets, navigates retribution and the febrile chaos of life in post-war Denmark.

Everytime

Sandra Wollner’s film, winner of Un Certain Regard at Cannes this year, is an enigmatic exploration of grief and the path to healing.

title_original: Interview: Ross McElwee on Remake
editorial_title_zh: 专访：罗斯·麦克埃尔维谈新片《重制》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 离海垂钓：这位纪录片导演谈起了他十多年来的第一部故事长片——一封倾注了情感震撼与复杂层次、写给儿子的信。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "自罗斯·麦克埃尔维（Ross McElwee）于1985年推出突破之作《谢尔曼的行军》（Sherman’s March）以来——在这部影片中，他一边笨拙地寻找女朋友，一边反思现代美国南方——这位纪录片导演便打磨出了一种苦乐参半、含蓄内敛的第一人称电影风格。他将镜头对准自己及身边人，以敏锐的幽默感和温和的抽离感，一再审视着自己的家庭生活和更广阔的世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《无限的时间》（Time Indefinite，1993）记录了他的第一次婚姻（对象为玛丽莲·莱文 Marilyn Levine）以及他们的儿子阿德里安（Adrian）的出生。在后来的影片中，我们看着阿德里安从一个惹人喜爱、温顺的儿子成长为焦躁不安的青少年；在《摄影记忆》（Photographic Memory，2011）中，我们看到他成为了一个与毒瘾挣扎的年轻成年人。令人心碎的是，阿德里安于2016年因芬太尼过量去世，年仅27岁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我曾经是个电影人，”麦克埃尔维在《重制》（Remake）的开场如是说，这也是他自《Photographic Memory》以来的首部纪录片。影片的大部分内容都是写给儿子的信——一封充满爱意、遗憾和未解之问的信。《重制》既有情感上的震撼，又兼具复杂的层次。罗斯借用了电影胶片放映时顺序错乱的比喻，带我们踏上了一段令人眼花缭乱的跨年代穿梭之旅，回溯了他的整个电影生涯、阿德里安自己的视频项目（比他父亲的更具动感和喧闹），以及这位年轻人的一生。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了阿德里安的故事，影片还详细讲述了好莱坞一次荒诞的尝试：他们曾误入歧途，企图将《谢尔曼的行军》重制为叙事电影，后来又改成了电视剧；此外还涉及罗斯与脑癌的搏斗——如果换作一部没那么悲剧的电影，这本会成为更大的事件；以及他与韩国纪录片导演金贤京看似幸福的婚姻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "考虑到题材的沉重与生猛，这部晚期生涯的杰作超越了一切阻碍，出自一位确实找到了自我重塑之道的电影人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "年轻的阿德里安在片中和你一起钓鱼时说的第一句话里，就提到他热爱“海洋的深邃惊喜”，因为你永远不知道自己会钓到什么。这正契合了你拍摄纪录片的方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一个绝妙的短语，特别是出自一个如此年轻的人之口。是的，这正是为什么我拥抱了这种笨拙而鲁莽的拍电影方式——你不去导演，不事先写好剧本，而是漫无目的地走入正在发生的事情中，然后看看有什么样的深邃惊喜在等待着。这就是[纪录片先驱]里奇·利科克（Ricky Leacock）过去常说的，看着一个时刻在镜头前绽放。我从来没有为自己的工作找到一个好的标签。我讨厌“个人纪录片”这个词，因为它听起来像除臭剂，但大家总是用它来描述我的作品。我的确在质疑，自己还能像这样继续拍多久，因为我认为这也是有代价的。你在从别人的生活中提取东西来构建你自己的电影。我只是希望，从我的电影中人们能隐约看到制片人对所拍摄之人的纯粹喜爱，即便这确实对这些人的个人生活造成了一点消耗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我们拍摄阿德里安时，能看到这种紧张感。我们看到他从你身边抽离，看到他的愤怒，但也能看到他对你的信任，看到他在试图自我救赎时向你敞开心扉。他一直在追随你，试图拍电影；他想做你正在做的事，但又想用不同的方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，我当然希望呈现出来的就是这种感觉。我也想说，是的，我在他长大的这些年里拍了很多次，但这只是我们相处时间里微不足道的一部分。在我拍电影的每一分钟背后，都有数不清的小时，我和他一起做着玩接球、辅导家庭作业之类的事情……如果没有我[在拍摄之外]倾注在他身上的时间，我想他是不会对我产生那种喜爱之情的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "弗雷德·维斯曼（Fred Wiseman）在几周前去世了，我一直在想他。你和他在电影创作方法上截然不同，但我认为你们的相通之处在于剪辑方式。无论是你的电影还是他的电影，在展现人物和讲述故事时都具有文学性。当然，不同之处在于，你和你的家人是影片的主角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我在大学的一门心理学课程上看过《提蒂库尔荒诞剧》（Titicut Follies，1967），以前从未见过那样的电影。它带着所有令人惊悚的回响一直留在我记忆深处。弗雷德的作品，以及那些早期的美国纪录片导演——里奇·利科克、梅索斯兄弟（Maysles Brothers）、D.A.彭内贝克（D.A. Pennebaker）——他们都触及了让我兴奋的东西。我曾与彭内贝克合作过他的电影《能源战争》（The Energy War，1979），讲的是天然气放松管制法案的通过，听起来这是世界上最无聊的话题。但无论是制作过程还是最终呈现，它都变得极其引人入胜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我对所有这些电影人都有着相似的联系。但在我涉足摄影和电影之前，我是一名作家。因此，创造这样一个人物化身——其声音对一部电影至关重要——让我感到非常自在。在某种程度上，这似乎很合适，它赋予了我拿起相机、毫无具体计划地闯入世界并进行拍摄的正当权利，就好像我是用自己的思想以及对所见之物的为主观反应来塑造这部电影一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想你在《重制》中的第一句画外音就是你说自己“曾经是个电影人”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这旨在表现一种悲哀的接受，即有些事情现在已经不同了。我并没有立刻说出那是什么。然后，在一组关于我儿子生平的蒙太奇镜头中，你得知他已经去世了。我真的不知道自己怎么还能继续当一个电影人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是如何坚持下来的？你在片中说，制作这部电影是让阿德里安活下去的一种方式。最令人印象深刻的是，你是如何设法退一步并如此优美地将其塑造出来的，这一定非常艰难。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这非常困难。我是如何走出低谷、尝试制作一部处理丧子之痛的电影的，方法是回归写作。我甚至无法着手去看那些素材或我的日记，因为实在太痛苦了。我雇了一位前助理，帮我过了一遍所有出现过阿德里安的电影，从《时光未决》开始，每部挑出一两帧画面。因为它们是静态图像，所以是定格的。这让我更容易构思该如何下笔来写这一切。我为他出现过的每部电影各写了一章，共七章。这帮我打破了僵局。一年后，我开始过素材。当我看到日积月累、断断续续拍下的那些素材加起来竟然有那么多时，我很惊讶。真的很多。而且在其中相当大一部分里，我的儿子都处于核心位置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，还有阿德里安自己的影像创作，它在你的电影中扮演了重要角色。剪辑他的素材想必很棘手吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "极其困难，因为他拍了一些非常不安的画面。他百无禁忌——他拍他的朋友们做着那些极难直视的事。有一个阶段，他还拍了自己注射海洛因的过程。我根本没法看。我让助理剪辑师挑出那些不那么难堪的素材；我想我在某种程度上仍然在保护他。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萦绕在我心头的一个真实问题是：如果这位纪录片导演父亲真的像他在片中反复表露的那样深爱他的儿子，为什么他会想要拍这样一部电影——在片中你能看到儿子一步步陷入可怕的毒瘾，以及毒瘾最终如何摧毁并夺去了他的生命？你为什么会想把这些捕捉到镜头里？你为什么会想要把它放进这部在很多方面都是关于你儿子的肖像片里？这是一个很难回答的问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一个回答是，这就是阿德里安人生的轨迹。你在片中看到了他的一生，你不得不把他人生的这一面也包含进来。我很好奇，你的电影创作有没有受到他的一些启发？你电影里的某些部分采用了非常具有创造性的剪辑手法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在那些段落、那些更像实验电影的蒙太奇中，倒不是那么明显。在我的电影里出现这种手法非常不寻常。阿德里安启发我的地方，在于他在自己拍摄的素材中对自己人生的诚实。我觉得那种诚实，无论好坏，都是我在自己的电影里没有运用的。我不会像他那样毫无保留地揭示自己生活中发生的一切。他拍摄一切、揭示自己生活中正在发生的事情时，毫无心理负担。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《重拍》这个片名内涵非常丰富。里面有对《谢尔曼的进军》那次未果的重拍，你也在某种程度上重拍了你的其他电影。你重组了婚姻。而且有人可能会说，儿子就是父亲的重拍版……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我希望它被理解的主要层面是：这部电影是我在失去儿子后，试图重塑我生活的尝试。这并不意味着悲伤或痛苦会消失。我只是接受了这样一个事实：余生你都得与它共存。但不知何故，这为我再次向前迈进扫清了道路。这就是我目前正在经历的，因为我开始习惯于与观众分享这部电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了向前看，还有回望。你有时会表达这样一种感觉：你拍摄的人们总是在变成他们自己的不同版本。你展示了你的第一场婚礼，并谈到那现在感觉像是一个虚构的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我想这就是我所说的回顾并重新评估我所拍摄素材的初衷。如今其中很多素材看起来几乎都成了虚构的：那真的是我吗？当人们问我，当我老去并回看那个年轻的自己——尤其是《谢尔曼的进军》时作何感想，我认为那不是我，那是我的弟弟。有点像个混蛋。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于《重拍》，我放映这部电影的地方还不多。而且全在国外。所以这一切都带着一种陌生和超脱尘世的意味。你知道的，在威尼斯的首映场放映期间，我崩溃了。而且看这部电影依然深深触动着我的情绪。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不知道我们谈论的这些事情会引发多少反对的声音。一个父亲拍摄自己的儿子。这是否与在心理上破坏他的稳定有关？是不是在无意中引诱他染上毒瘾？我不知道；你可以这样争辩。我并不真的认为自己有罪，但我的内心深处又觉得或许我确实有。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在电影里并没有这种感觉。到了快结束时，阿德里安处于一种感到绝望、指望你来帮忙的时刻。当他跟你说话时，人们会觉得他知道自己同时也是在对可能看到这些的观众说话。那种坦诚非常感人。这听起来可能有点琐碎，但你对这部电影满意吗？你能纯粹把它当作一件作品来欣赏吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这很难。再多放映四五场后，它就会更接近那种状态了。我会允许自己享受完成电影并把它推向世界所能带来的任何满足感。剪辑师乔·比尼（Joe Bini）曾与沃纳·赫尔佐格合作过20多部电影，他介入进来，为我提供了我靠自己无法召集的对这部电影的客观视角。我的制片人马克·梅亚托（Mark Meatto）在电影演进过程中一直坚定地支持我。而我的妻子是这部电影粗剪版问世时唯一看过的人。这三人帮助[我]找到了完成电影所需的客观性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不剧透给那些还没机会看这部电影的观众，但在《重拍》结尾处，《谢尔曼的进军》那种实际且奇迹般的重拍方式，是一个迹象，表明你的电影在某种程度上得到了庇佑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那太疯狂了。而且美妙。它就那么凭空出现了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就像你在海里捕获的东西一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没错。它直接把你带回了起点。这究竟是从哪来的？海洋深处的惊奇。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since Ross McElwee’s 1985 breakthrough Sherman’s March , in which he narrated his bumbling search for a girlfriend alongside reflections on the modern American South, the documentarian has honed a wry, understated form of first-person cinema. Turning the camera on himself and on those around him, he’s repeatedly observed his domestic life and the larger world with keen humor and gentle detachment."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Time Indefinite (1993) documented his first marriage, to Marilyn Levine, and the birth of their son, Adrian. In subsequent films, we watched Adrian grow from adorable and adoring son to restless teen; in Photographic Memory (2011), we saw him as a young adult struggling with addiction. Tragically, Adrian died of a fentanyl overdose in 2016 at 27 years of age."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I used to be a filmmaker,” McElwee tells us at the start of Remake , his first documentary since Photographic Memory. Much of the film is a letter to his son—a letter filled with love, regret, and unanswered questions. Remake is as emotionally devastating as it is intricately layered. Employing the metaphor of a film whose reels are projected out of order, Ross takes us on a dizzying trip back and forth across the decades, journeying through his filmography, Adrian’s own video projects (much more kinetic and rambunctious than his father’s), and the young man’s entire lifespan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alongside Adrian’s story, the film also details the absurd saga of a misguided Hollywood attempt to remake Sherman’s March as a narrative feature and then as a TV series; Ross’s bout with brain cancer, which would be a bigger deal in a less tragic film; and his seemingly happy marriage to Korean documentary filmmaker Hyun kyung Kim."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Against all odds, given the rawness of its subject matter, it is a late-career masterpiece by a filmmaker who has indeed found a way to remake himself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the first things that a young Adrian says in the film, as you both are fishing, is how he loves “the deep surprise of the ocean” because you don’t know what you’re going to catch. That speaks to your approach to documentary filmmaking."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s such a marvelous phrase, especially coming out of the mouth of someone so young. And yes, it is very much why I embraced this awkward and foolhardy way of making films, where you don’t direct, you don’t script things in advance—you wander into things happening and then see what kinds of deep surprises are waiting. It’s what [documentary pioneer] Ricky Leacock used to call watching a moment bloom right in front of the camera. I’ve never found a good label for what I do. I hate the phrase “personal documentary” because it sounds like a deodorant, but it’s used all the time to describe my work. I do question how much I’ll be able to continue to film like that, because I think there’s also a price to be paid. You are extracting something from other people’s lives to build your own films. I would just hope that somehow what’s gleaned from seeing my films is the filmmaker’s unalloyed affection for the people he’s filming, even if it is exacting a bit of a toll on people’s personal lives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We see some of this tension when you film Adrian. We see him pull away from you, we see his anger, but we also see his trust in you, in the way he opens up to you when he’s trying to cure himself. And he’s following you, trying to make films; he wants to do what you’re doing, but differently."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Well, I certainly hope that’s how it comes across. I also feel like saying that, yes, I filmed him a lot over the years of him growing up, but it was a tiny portion of our time together. For every minute of filming there were hours and hours where I was with him doing things like playing catch and helping with homework . . . Without the time that I lavished on him [outside of the filming], I don’t think the affection would have been there on his part."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fred Wiseman died a few weeks ago, and I’ve been thinking about him a lot. You and he are very different in your approaches to filmmaking, but where I think you’re linked is in the way that you edit. Both your films and his are literary in the way they reveal character and tell stories. What’s different with your work, of course, is that you and your family members are the subjects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I saw Titicut Follies (1967) in a psychology course in college, and I’d never seen anything like that film before. It stayed with me in all of its horrifying resonance. Fred’s work, and those early American documentary filmmakers—Ricky Leacock, the Maysles Brothers, D.A. Pennebaker—were all onto something that excited me. I worked with Pennebaker on his film The Energy War (1979), about the passage of a natural-gas deregulation bill, which sounds like the most boring topic in the world. But it became something really fascinating, both to make and then to see."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I have similar connections to all of these filmmakers. But before I got into photography and film, I was a writer. So creating this persona of someone whose voice was important to a film was something I felt very comfortable doing. It seemed appropriate, in a way, to earn the right to hold a camera and go into the world and film without a real plan, as if I shaped the film with my thoughts and my subjective responses to what I was seeing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I think your first line of voiceover in Remake is you saying you “used to be a filmmaker.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That’s meant to be a kind of mournful acceptance of the fact that something’s different now. article_text:
Since Ross McElwee’s 1985 breakthrough Sherman’s March , in which he narrated his bumbling search for a girlfriend alongside reflections on the modern American South, the documentarian has honed a wry, understated form of first-person cinema. Turning the camera on himself and on those around him, he’s repeatedly observed his domestic life and the larger world with keen humor and gentle detachment.

Time Indefinite (1993) documented his first marriage, to Marilyn Levine, and the birth of their son, Adrian. In subsequent films, we watched Adrian grow from adorable and adoring son to restless teen; in Photographic Memory (2011), we saw him as a young adult struggling with addiction. Tragically, Adrian died of a fentanyl overdose in 2016 at 27 years of age.

“I used to be a filmmaker,” McElwee tells us at the start of Remake , his first documentary since Photographic Memory. Much of the film is a letter to his son—a letter filled with love, regret, and unanswered questions. Remake is as emotionally devastating as it is intricately layered. Employing the metaphor of a film whose reels are projected out of order, Ross takes us on a dizzying trip back and forth across the decades, journeying through his filmography, Adrian’s own video projects (much more kinetic and rambunctious than his father’s), and the young man’s entire lifespan.

Alongside Adrian’s story, the film also details the absurd saga of a misguided Hollywood attempt to remake Sherman’s March as a narrative feature and then as a TV series; Ross’s bout with brain cancer, which would be a bigger deal in a less tragic film; and his seemingly happy marriage to Korean documentary filmmaker Hyun kyung Kim.

Against all odds, given the rawness of its subject matter, it is a late-career masterpiece by a filmmaker who has indeed found a way to remake himself.

One of the first things that a young Adrian says in the film, as you both are fishing, is how he loves “the deep surprise of the ocean” because you don’t know what you’re going to catch. That speaks to your approach to documentary filmmaking.

It’s such a marvelous phrase, especially coming out of the mouth of someone so young. And yes, it is very much why I embraced this awkward and foolhardy way of making films, where you don’t direct, you don’t script things in advance—you wander into things happening and then see what kinds of deep surprises are waiting. It’s what [documentary pioneer] Ricky Leacock used to call watching a moment bloom right in front of the camera. I’ve never found a good label for what I do. I hate the phrase “personal documentary” because it sounds like a deodorant, but it’s used all the time to describe my work. I do question how much I’ll be able to continue to film like that, because I think there’s also a price to be paid. You are extracting something from other people’s lives to build your own films. I would just hope that somehow what’s gleaned from seeing my films is the filmmaker’s unalloyed affection for the people he’s filming, even if it is exacting a bit of a toll on people’s personal lives.

We see some of this tension when you film Adrian. We see him pull away from you, we see his anger, but we also see his trust in you, in the way he opens up to you when he’s trying to cure himself. And he’s following you, trying to make films; he wants to do what you’re doing, but differently.

Well, I certainly hope that’s how it comes across. I also feel like saying that, yes, I filmed him a lot over the years of him growing up, but it was a tiny portion of our time together. For every minute of filming there were hours and hours where I was with him doing things like playing catch and helping with homework . . . Without the time that I lavished on him [outside of the filming], I don’t think the affection would have been there on his part.

Fred Wiseman died a few weeks ago, and I’ve been thinking about him a lot. You and he are very different in your approaches to filmmaking, but where I think you’re linked is in the way that you edit. Both your films and his are literary in the way they reveal character and tell stories. What’s different with your work, of course, is that you and your family members are the subjects.

I saw Titicut Follies (1967) in a psychology course in college, and I’d never seen anything like that film before. It stayed with me in all of its horrifying resonance. Fred’s work, and those early American documentary filmmakers—Ricky Leacock, the Maysles Brothers, D.A. Pennebaker—were all onto something that excited me. I worked with Pennebaker on his film The Energy War (1979), about the passage of a natural-gas deregulation bill, which sounds like the most boring topic in the world. But it became something really fascinating, both to make and then to see.

I have similar connections to all of these filmmakers. But before I got into photography and film, I was a writer. So creating this persona of someone whose voice was important to a film was something I felt very comfortable doing. It seemed appropriate, in a way, to earn the right to hold a camera and go into the world and film without a real plan, as if I shaped the film with my thoughts and my subjective responses to what I was seeing.

I think your first line of voiceover in Remake is you saying you “used to be a filmmaker.”

That’s meant to be a kind of mournful acceptance of the fact that something’s different now. I don’t say what that is right away. And then you learn in a montage of moments from my son’s life that he’s dead. I didn’t really see how I could continue to be a filmmaker.

How did you continue? You say in the film that making it was a way of keeping Adrian alive. What’s so impressive is how you were somehow able to step back and shape it so beautifully, which must have been so difficult.

It was very difficult. How I turned the corner, to try to make some sort of a film that dealt with the loss of my son, was that I reverted to writing. I couldn’t even begin to go through the films or my diary because it was just too painful. I hired a former assistant to go through all my films that feature Adrian and choose one or two frames from each, beginning with Time Indefinite . Because they were still images, they were frozen. That made it easier for me to think of how I could possibly begin to write about this. I wrote seven chapters, for each of the films in which he’d appeared. That enabled me to break the ice. A year later, I started going through the footage. I was surprised when I saw how much just filming a little bit now and then added up over the years. There was a lot. And my son was front and center in an awful lot of it.

And of course, there’s Adrian’s own filmmaking, which plays an important role in your film. I guess it was tricky to edit his footage.

It was extremely difficult because he filmed some very disturbing things. There were no holds barred—he filmed his friends doing things that were very difficult to watch. He filmed himself at one point while injecting heroin. I couldn’t look at it. I had an assistant editor choose the less difficult footage; I think I was still trying to protect him in a way.

A real question that haunts me is if the filmmaker-father truly loves his son as much as he declares that he does throughout the film, why would he want to make a film in which you see the son spiraling into this dreadful addiction, and how it ultimately affected him and then killed him? Why would you want that captured on film? And why would you want that in what is in many ways a portrait of your son? That’s a hard question to answer.

One answer is that this is the shape of Adrian’s life. You see the entirety of his life in the film, and you had to include this side of his story. I was curious if you were inspired at all by his filmmaking? There are some sections in your movie that use a very inventive editing approach.

Not so much in those passages, those montages, which are more like experimental filmmaking. It’s very unusual to have that in my films. What inspired me about Adrian was his honesty about his own life in the footage that he shot. I felt that kind of honesty is something that, for better or for worse, I do not utilize in my films. I don’t reveal everything that’s going on in my life the way he does. He just had no problem filming everything and revealing what was going on in his life.

The title Remake is so rich. There’s the attempted remake of Sherman’s March , and you’re remaking your other films in a way. You’ve remade your marriage. And one might say a son is a remake of a father…

The primary way that I mean for it to be interpreted is that the film is my attempt to remake my life after losing my son. That doesn’t mean that the grief or the pain goes away. I just accept the fact that you live with that for the rest of your life. But somehow it clears the way for me to move forward again. That’s what I’m going through right now, as I’m beginning to get used to sharing the film with audiences.

In addition to moving forward, there’s also a look back. You sometimes express the feeling that the people you film are always becoming different versions of themselves. You show your first wedding, and talk about how that feels like a fiction now.

I think that’s what I meant by my intention of going back and reassessing the footage I’ve shot. A lot of it at this point does seem almost fictional: is that really me? When people ask me what I think of myself as I grow older and look back on the younger person, especially Sherman’s March , I think that wasn’t me, that was my younger brother. Sort of an asshole.

With Remake , there have only been a few places where I’ve shown the film. And all in foreign countries. So it all has that quotient of being strange and otherworldly. You know, I broke down during a screening in Venice during the premiere. And it still deeply affects me emotionally to watch it.

I wonder how much pushback I’ll get from some of the things we’ve been talking about. A father filming his son. Did that have anything to do with destabilizing him psychologically? Unconsciously leading him into drug addiction? I don’t know; you could argue that. I don’t really think that’s what I’m guilty of, but some part of me thinks maybe I am.

It doesn’t feel like that in the film. Toward the end, Adrian is at a point where he feels hopeless and he’s looking to you to help. When he’s talking to you, one feels like he knows that he’s also talking to the audience that might be seeing this. There is an openness that’s really touching. This is going to sound trivial, perhaps, but are you satisfied with the film? Can you just appreciate it as a work?

It’s hard. With another four or five screenings, it’ll start to become more like that. I’ll allow myself whatever satisfaction is to be had from finishing the film and getting it out there. The editor Joe Bini, who did 20-plus films with Werner Herzog, came in and gave me perspective on the film that I wasn’t able to summon on my own. My producer Mark Meatto stood by me as the film evolved. And my wife was the only person to see the film when it was a rough cut. Those three helped [me] find the objectivity needed to finish the film.

I won’t spoil it for viewers who haven’t had the chance to see the film yet, but the actual, and miraculous, way that Sherman’s March is remade toward the end of Remake is a sign that your film was blessed in some way.

That was insane. And wonderful. And it came out of nowhere.

Like what you catch in the ocean.

Exactly. It takes you right back to the beginning. Where did this come from? The deep surprise of the ocean.
excerpt_original: Gone fishing: the documentarian talks about his first feature in over a decade, an emotionally devastating and intricately layered letter to his son

article_text:
News

Róng Museum of Art Reveals Its Curatorial Team

FREYA CHOU ,

LI JIA , and

SUSANNA ZHU . Photo by niuniufilm. Courtesy the Róng Museum of Art, Shenzhen.

Shenzhen’s Róng Museum of Art (RMoA) has appointed Freya Chou, Li Jia, and Susanna Zhu as members of its curatorial team. They will join Pi Li , RMoA’s founding director, in shaping the museum’s research initiatives, exhibitions, and public programs ahead of its scheduled opening in mid-2027.

Based in Hong Kong, Freya Chou is known for exploring intercultural exchange across various disciplines, from visual art and performance to literature. From 2015 to 2019, she served as the inaugural curator of education and public programs at Hong Kong’s nonprofit Para Site, and has overseen projects at various institutions across the globe, including the Taipei Fine Arts Museum, the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh, and Turin’s Museum of Asian Art. She headed Hong Kong’s presentation at the 59th Venice Biennale (2022), co-curated the 13th Taipei Biennial (2023), and most recently curated Ellen Pau ’s retrospective at the SculptureCenter in New York, titled “She Moves.”

In her curatorial practice, Li Jia engages with cross-generational contemporary artists from China and across Asia. After helming Pace Gallery’s Beijing branch as deputy director from 2012 to 2015, she joined the Taikang Art Museum (formerly Taikang Space) as senior curator from 2015 to 2020, where she organized numerous presentations, including Yang Guangnan’s “Light Pavilion Project” (2016–18) and “Genders Engender” (2018). At RMoA, she and Chou will be in charge of developing the museum’s exhibitions and research endeavors.

Susanna Zhu brings more than two decades of experience to her new role. She previously worked as deputy director of the Shenzhen Fine Art Institute’s exhibition department from 2003 to 2014, as well as secretary general of the Shenzhen Curiosity Museum Studies Centre from 2017 to 2026. Over the past two years, she was the director of the Zishi Garden Community Museum of Sustainability. Zhu will lead RMoA’s public engagement initiatives and learning programs.

In a press release, Pi Li stated, “Freya Chou, Li Jia, and Susanna Zhu each bring substantial expertise and distinct perspectives. . . . Their appointments further strengthen the museum’s professional team and will help us build a curatorial and research framework that is both intellectually rigorous and open in spirit, laying an important foundation for the museum’s opening.”

Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: Freya Chou, Li Jia, and Susanna Zhu join the Shenzhen institution ahead of its 2027 opening. Harison Butler

article_text:
A federal judge has thrown out a whistleblower lawsuit that accused the Los Angeles Film School of massive student loan fraud and has sanctioned the claimants’ attorney for filing a brief generated by ChatGPT.

The whistleblowers, two former executives at the school, filed a false claims suit in 2024, alleging a scheme in which the school paid outside vendors to hire its own students, inflating its job placement figures. The school paid $1 million to resolve a Department of Education audit into that and other issues in 2020, but the executives alleged that the school had lied to DOE investigators and hidden the full scope of the fraud.

Tom DeSimone, Director of 'Chatterbox,' 'Reform School Girls,' Dies at 87

In a ruling issued Friday , Judge Stanley Blumenfeld dismissed the suit with prejudice, finding that much of the alleged conduct fell outside the six-year statute of limitations. He also imposed a $5,000 fine on attorney Mark Kleiman for submitting a brief without disclosing that it had been written by AI.

The 76-page brief , filed in April, cited a non-existent case, Darwich v. Department of Economic Security. It also cited two additional cases that were real but did not support the proposition for which they were advanced — one of which was authored by Blumenfeld.

One of the claimants, Dave Phillips, later acknowledged that he had drafted the brief himself using ChatGPT and given it to his attorney to review. Kleiman submitted the brief with a disclaimer attempting to disavow any involvement in it other than to file it to meet a deadline. The attorney later explained to the court that his relationships with Phillips and with the other claimant, Ben Chaib, had broken down.

A week after submitting the brief, Kleiman told opposition counsel that his clients had written it with AI and that he was going to withdraw from the case.

In issuing sanctions, the judge faulted Kleiman for “a sustained pattern of neglect” and for violations of court orders and of ethical standards.

“Kleiman filed an obviously deficient brief that he had not even fully read and for which he did not check whether the citations were to real cases — let alone that they supported the brief’s assertions — despite knowing that his nonlawyer clients had prepared the brief using AI,” the judge wrote.

Granting the school’s motion to dismiss, the judge found that the AI-generated opposition brief “contains almost no citations to legal authority or to the (complaint), and advances legal arguments that appear untethered to the (False Claims Act) or Ninth Circuit law.”

The judge also faulted Phillips and Chaib for not getting a new attorney months earlier, when the relationship began to deteriorate. He noted that they were “not blameless” in the AI use, but elected not to sanction them because they are not lawyers.

Phillips, a former VP of job placement at L.A. Film School, and Chaib, former VP of admissions, accused the school of hoodwinking its students and the government by artificially inflating job placement stats. The suit alleged that the school knew its graduates rarely went on to a career in film or music, quoting an internal document stating that most graduates “report a yearly income of 0-$5,000 in their field of study.”

According to the complaint, the school paid entities including Ivar Music Group to hire its students for two-day jobs. The suit alleged that LAFS had used the inflated placement stats to maintain accreditation and eligibility for federal student loans.

The suit also included allegations against CEO James “Bill” Heavener, who owns LAFS and Full Sail University in Winter Park, Fla. Though the complaint alleged that Full Sail University was part of the fraud, the judge found that the claimants had failed to offer any details pertaining to that school.

Other for-profit colleges have paid out multimillion-dollar settlements to resolve suits under the False Claims Act, which allows whistleblowers to sue for fraud against the government and to claim a share of the payout.

Kleiman did not respond to a request for comment.

article_text:
Films and events

Dare

At Night

Beatrice Gibson’s feature directorial debut is a luminous nocturne, evocatively capturing the streets of Paris over the course of a single night on 16mm.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Beatrice Gibson

With Diocouda Diaoune, Kátia Belo Cardoso, Sophie Robinson

UK-France 2026. 87min

Courtesy of Somesuch

Languages English, French, Bambara, Mandarin Chinese With some English subtitles

Introduction

Inspired by the poetry of Alice Notley and other avant-garde literary figures, At Night moves with Gibson and a group of women in their forties as they share intimate reflections on desire, creativity, motherhood, sexuality and identity. Blending chance encounters, lived experiences and imagined worlds, it unfolds as a poetic, oneiric tapestry of voices, memories and possibilities, carried along by a hypnotic synth score.

Hyun Jin Cho

Content advice

Contains scenes of nudity.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Chronovisor

The film collective Cosmic Salon (Jack Auen and Kevin Walker) make their beguiling and assured feature debut, guiding us through hidden histories and uncanny landscapes of belief, mystery and the unknown.

Tropical Fractals

Leonardo Pirondi’s timely reflection on ecological collapse imagines a future in which a biodome spaceship preserves the last traces of life on Earth.

The Last Day

Acclaimed visual artist Rachel Rose gives Mrs Dalloway a contemporary makeover in her arresting mood piece, starring Alicia Vikander and Victoria Pedretti.
