article_text:
Barry Keoghan is making headlines for appearing in a new social media video shared by U.K. celebrity facial expert and Dermaspa founder Nilam Holmes, who posted a behind-the-scenes look at the Oscar nominee’s Xerf treatment. Per Dermaspa’s website , Xerf forgoes injections and uses radio-frequency technology to tighten the skin and renew collagen. The treatment costs around $3,500 for a face and neck session.

“I’ve been working with Barry for a while now, looking after his skin through different movies, campaigns and projects and the trust he places in me means a lot,” Holmes wrote in a caption accompanying the video. “His skin has really improved over the last few years and he looks great. Today we did his [second Xerf] skin-tightening treatment. I was running late filming some Xerf content, so rather than make me rush what I was doing, he offered to let me film him having it.”

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

Keoghan narrates the video, saying: “I’ve been hearing a lot about it, and Nilam is very excited about it, and she’s great at what she does. I really mean that, and again, every time I come in, it’s very relaxing and therapeutic. I feel better about myself, I look better. I think it’s important to look after yourself inside and outside.”

As seen on Holmes’ social media pages, her other clients who have undergone Xerf treatment include Chris Appleton, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Joe Alwyn and Nicole Scherzinger. She’s also worked with Pink and Joe Alwyn and has posted regularly about treating Keoghan in the past, giving him facials before various photo shoots.

“Working on multiple projects at a time; movies, campaigns, interviews, press and philanthropy projects means unstructured routine, travel, make up, and disrupted sleep patterns, which all take a toll on the skin,” Holmes posted in March 2025 about treating Keoghan for his Wonderland magazine cover. “So we have regular skin sessions which consist of fixing up problematic skin, calming down inflammation, maintaining the skin when it’s great and trying to get that healthy, rested look. On top of that Barry is like a little student for me. Passionate about everything, he likes to know everything about everything which I love and he brings the fun when he visits.”

Earlier this year, Keoghan went viral for telling SiriusXM’s “The Morning Mash Up” that the online “abuse” about his appearance had gotten so bad that he no longer wanted to “go outside.”

“There’s a lot of hate online,” Keoghan explained at the time. “There’s a lot of abuse of how I look, and it’s kind of past the point of — you know, everyone goes through that… but it’s made me shy away. It’s made me really go inside myself, not want to attend places, not want to go outside. I say this being absolute pure and honest to you. It’s becoming a problem.”

Keoghan noted that he removed himself from social media to avoid nasty comments about himself, but occasionally, after a premiere or event, he would go online to see “how he’s received.” Unfortunately, he said most of the time, the reaction is “not nice.”

article_text:
Feature

Let’s Give a Round of A-Paws to These Tompkins Dog Parade Participants

Santa Paws, Vincent van Doge, and the papal Pup Leo were among this year’s fierce competition.

Hyperallergic )

Every fall, the East Village gets all furry-scurry as hundreds of dogs and their doting families race to the Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade. Despite the chill that descended upon New York on Saturday, October 17, spectators and participants braced the winds to cheer on entries spanning "Pup Leo," a Yayoi Kusama pumpkin, a cyclosporiasis parasite, and an entourage of Pomeranians dripped out in Knicks gear.

Event organizers for the parade's 36th iteration welcomed the normal flurry of advertisements while placing a particular emphasis on shelter adoptions, bringing 250 dogs looking for new homes to the parade. There was fierce competition among the around 500 participating pups and their equally committed parents, who moseyed their way from East 13th Street and Avenue B down to Tompkins Square Park. Spectators perched themselves on lampposts and CitiBike seats behind the barricades to watch the march, while a few lucky locals watched the festivity from their fire escapes.

The second iteration since longtime organizer Joseph Borduin stepped down from his post in 2024, this year's event was arranged by the nonprofit New York Dog Parade and was sponsored by Kismet, the pet food brand co-founded by celebrity couple John Legend and Chrissy Teigen.

Many of the paw -ticipants were also in the running for the annual costume contest. Edging out stiff competition including a pug poking out of a wheel of cheese on a charcuterie board and a Bad Bunny-themed float, a Shih Tzu dressed as Knicks captain Jalen Brunson took home first prize.

article_text:
“It’s pouring rain, so it’s beautiful. The land needed it.” Paul Nicklen picks up the phone in Kenya, slightly out of breath, after it buzzed for a long time at the bottom of a pocket. He and his wife, the photographer Cristina Mittermeier, have just moved onto the lands of Segera, in the heart of Laikipia, and the house is still full of boxes. The week before, he flew his new plane, a Super Cub, a small high-winged bush plane, all the way from South Africa himself. A strange destination for a man of the poles, who long kept the continent at arm’s length, out of clear-sightedness. “It’s so beautiful, and it’s been photographed so heavily by my peers at National Geographic , and so many good photographers, like Nick Brandt, have worked here,” he explains. “I knew the second I came to Africa that I would fall in love with it and it would be hard to keep me away.” A correct prediction. A first flight over the savanna, love at first sight, a plane ordered on the spot. It looks a lot like the way he works: long patience, then momentum.

Reverence begins with a trail. The one Louise Jeannine Roy, Paul Nicklen’s mother, climbed every morning for 15 years on Vancouver Island, up to a clearing overlooking the Strait of Georgia. A septuagenarian in top shape, a realtor, a dancer in her kitchen to the sound of Leonard Cohen, she died of a brain tumor. A few weeks later, behind the wheel, her son still asked Siri to call Mom. Then he made the climb alone, with the two dogs rescued from the beaches of Baja California, and performed his mother’s ritual: turning toward the four directions. To the east, his parents and the Saskatchewan farm, where every summer a calf became his friend before disappearing. To the north, Kimmirut, on Baffin Island, an Inuit village of 190 people, with no telephone, no television, no radio, where the boy whistled at the northern lights to make them come closer. To the south, 20 years of assignments for National Geographic . To the west, British Columbia and SeaLegacy, the organization he founded with Cristina. A table of contents, in short, drawn by a compass.

Hence the first chapter, “Matriarchs.” “I’ve spent my lifetime around wildlife and animals,” says Paul Nicklen. “It’s one thing to be a big male out there just surviving and breeding and eating. And then I just think of the hardships mothers go through.” He mentions polar bears, the females fasting all summer on land like the males, then shutting themselves in their dens for another four months without food, long enough to give birth and nurse. “I’m just in awe of females.” The image that truly opens the book shows what he means: in Tonga, a humpback whale cradles her calf under her chin above a white sandy bottom, a ring of remoras around her belly like a hula dancer’s grass skirt. That day, the photographer stayed for three hours, making some 40 breath-hold dives of 90 seconds each, until the mother slid the tip of her pectoral fin, more than 15 feet long, between them. A boundary drawn, a boundary respected. “No photograph is ever worth stressing out or upsetting an animal,” he says. When he climbed back onto the boat at sunset, the whale and her calf had not moved an inch.

Curiously, the foreword is signed by Mother Earth. The device could seem naive, but it turns out to be delightfully frank, since the planet catches her portraitist red-handed in his clumsiness: “I have watched him fumble on the ice, misjudge the light, and surface from my waters with empty frames.” Paul Nicklen owns it. “I probably fail 98% of the time, and that’s just part of the journey. I think it’s beautiful in a way.” He recalls an encounter in the Azores with a 90-foot female blue whale, capable of engulfing the volume of an Olympic swimming pool in a single mouthful, of which no image found its way into the book.

It all began with a blur. At 15, on a family trip to Italy, his mother, a schoolteacher and amateur photographer who had set up a darkroom at home, lent him her Pentax K1000. At 18, as a biology student at the University of Victoria, Paul Nicklen still struggled to get his pictures in focus. Bad grades too, for lack of concentration in class: he only discovered much later that he has attention deficit disorder. A late focus. A curious paradox for a man capable of waiting five years for narwhals, and who only sits still on the ice or underwater. His eye was born after his studies, in the Barren Lands, the vast tundra between Nunavut and the Northwest Territories, where a pilot dropped him off alone for three months. More than 600 miles on foot and by canoe, 50 pounds lost, wolves, musk oxen, a golden eagles’ nest. “I felt like a wild animal myself,” he sums up. Then came his mentors, Flip Nicklin and Joel Sartore, and National Geographic .

His signature comes down to one word: proximity. Paul Nicklen works up close, often with a wide-angle lens, the animal filling the frame. His emperor penguins bursting out of the water were shot at 16-35mm, at 1/1250th of a second. The dome port of his underwater housing bears the marks of his subjects: a sperm whale calf gummed it like a puppy, a female leopard seal confronted her own reflection in it, jaws wide open. Hence his fondness for a very different temperament, that of Vincent Munier, with his mists and distant silhouettes captured with a telephoto lens. He showed Munier’s work in his SoHo gallery in New York, hailing “the extremely talented Vincent Munier,” while knowing that this way of seeing belongs to the Frenchman from the Vosges. His own art rests on a kind of humility before error. “I’ve made so many mistakes around them, and they’re so forgiving,” he recently told his alma mater. “They look at your stupidity, and they just sort of casually walk around you.” His images? “I’m proud of my pictures, but I don’t ever look at my pictures and go, wow, those are good. I think nature is perfect.” Only one hangs in his home: the polar bear at the cabin window.

He edited the book alone, facing his archive: 2.5 million photographs taken over 30 years. “With National Geographic , you thought about the story first, and then often with a lot of books, you think about the geography, whether it’s the Arctic or Antarctic or the Serengeti Plains. And for me, I didn’t care.” Emotion alone counts, hence chapters titled like poems, “Ancient Wisdom,” “Emerald Seas,” “Other Nations,” and a free flow from one continent to another. The captions are moved to the back of the book, letting the spreads breathe in the large format (12.5 by 15 inches, 360 pages, printed in Paris by Printmodel). What follows reads like a family album: a coastal wolf pup, proud as a page boy, carrying an eagle feather almost as long as itself (British Columbia); a lion cub staring at its reflection in the lens (Namiri Plains, Tanzania); Craig, the last of the great elephants whose tusks reached the ground, who died of old age at 54 (Amboseli, Kenya); a polar bear poking her head through a cabin window in the middle of a blizzard, lit by the screen of a laptop the photographer holds in his left hand (Svalbard). A stroke of genius.

There is also Ma’ah, “grandmother” in Sm’algyax, the language of the Gitga’at. Paul Nicklen searched for this Kermode bear, a variety of black bear with white fur, sacred to the First Nations, as early as 1997, without success. Another failure in 2009. In 2010, a few days were enough, thanks to the Gitga’at and the guide Marven Robinson: Ma’ah appeared among the red clusters of a crabapple tree, the image made the cover of National Geographic , and the Northern Gateway pipeline project, which would have brought oil tankers into these fjords, was eventually abandoned thanks to activists, scientists and Indigenous communities. Nine years later, he found her again, the fur thinning around her eyes. “It’s the first time I’ve really had a chance to publish my spirit bear pictures inside a book,” he says. Ma’ah, for her part, still has no idea of the role she played.

He is sometimes called “too National Geographic ,” a prisoner of the spectacular. The facts tell another story. With more than 7 million followers on Instagram, Paul Nicklen is the most followed wildlife photographer on the platform, and one of the most followed photographers in the world, all genres combined. In Hartley Bay, the Gitga’at elder Helen Clifton held up the magazine with Ma’ah on the cover and told him: “We did this together.” Among the Inuit, he learned to listen more, talk less and never brag. The acknowledgments in Reverence run for pages, naming his Inuit companions from Canada and Greenland, the Maasai guides who led him to Craig, pilots, captains, and three late friends whose laughter he will never forget. He locates his loneliness elsewhere: in hotel rooms in big cities, after giving talks. “When I’m in nature, I’m never lonely.” As for National Geographic , he owes it everything, and left it for precisely that reason: “It’s great to have 100 million people plus see your story on National Geographic , but if you’re not affecting change, then what’s the point?” Hence SeaLegacy, the SoHo gallery, the fine art prints, and this book whose cover, a whale and her calf in black and white, has more of the print than of the documentary plate.

Another long wait. For 30 years, Paul Nicklen dreamed of getting close to a puma. On Vancouver Island, home to the densest cougar population in the world, he had only glimpsed one, scurrying back into the brush. In Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, his guide Rodrigo Moraga led him to a young female he had known since she was born. A snowstorm rose, and they sheltered in the same cave. “She never looked at me once. She was just looking across the valley waiting for guanacos to come out during a storm so she could go hunting,” he remembers. As she left, she brushed against his leg, “basically zero centimeters away.” Tears. Rodrigo smiled and simply said: “I know.” The emotion, the photographer explains, lies above all in the place: an estancia that decided these cats, long shot by ranchers, were worth more alive. “Now to see 10 a day, it’s really special.” In the book, we meet Petaka, another female, lying beneath a rainbow or looking up at an Andean condor with the nonchalance of a queen.

The poles remain his kingdom. His emperor penguins bursting from the water in a trail of microbubbles, an image that won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition in 2011, came from a tip by his Swedish friend Göran Ehlmé, who had filmed the phenomenon ten years earlier for the BBC. Nicklen barely believed it. Two and a half months alone on the Antarctic sea ice, diving whenever possible, until the day the birds released the air from their feathers and rocketed to the surface. Older still, the narwhal saga lasted five years: a parasail towed by a snowmobile, a fall into a meltwater pool, an ultralight flown with his high school friend Brian Knutsen, and finally, landed on a single ice floe, a thousand tusks breaking the surface. Right after, the rotten ice gave way beneath his feet and his shoulder was dislocated; it took nearly an hour to put it back in place. He smiled the whole time. The shoulder was replaced last summer.

These images fund everything else. “Everything I do is sort of the intersection of art, science and conservation,” sums up Paul Nicklen, who makes his living selling his prints. It has to be beautiful, grounded in fact, and moving. Such as his ice waterfall, meltwater pouring off the Nordaustlandet ice cap in Svalbard, which Pearl Jam chose for the cover of their 2020 album Gigaton . Or his aerial views, almost watercolors: tannin-stained rivers winding between the white dunes of Lençóis Maranhenses in Brazil, the branching channels of the Colorado River Delta in Mexico, where the river no longer reaches the sea.

Seen from above, everything is reframed. And with all due reverence, Paul Nicklen dares to say what many believers will find provocative. “People live their lives on this planet as if they’re gonna go see some dude in a white robe waiting for them, and they often are disrespectful of this planet. For me, I’ve always said heaven is here and now.” He remembers a dinner with Elon Musk and his horror at the Martian dream: “That’s hell. Like, to live with a bunch of humans under a glass dome, with air that you can’t breathe, there’s no water to drink. Where is the romance in that when you think of 4 billion years arriving at this point with this incredibly precious planet?”

And artificial intelligence, capable of generating a pod of narwhals in seconds? “I can spot AI pretty easily, and I’m not too worried about it,” he replies. His sadness goes to young photographers starting out in this new world. “It’s more, what is the story worth? What is honest journalism? Using powerful photography to bring people into the conversation.” Why, then, wonder rather than alarm, when the book points out that wildlife populations have fallen by nearly 70% in 50 years? “Hope is the only emotion really greater than fear.” What he hopes for from the reader follows from this, and fits in a few words: close the book, go outside, look around, and let that beauty weigh on everyday choices. He has not forgotten the starving polar bear filmed in 2017 and seen by a quarter of the planet, and he argues for mixing registers. Still, Reverence leans firmly toward wonder, down to the tiny creatures of the Lembeh Strait in Indonesia, explored at night on a rebreather: an emperor shrimp riding a nudibranch, an octopus hauling two halves of a shell like a caravan and shutting itself in at the slightest doubt. Breathtaking.

This wonder comes from far away, from the boy of Kimmirut and his long nights without television, when stories were told in stone. “I saw beluga whales in carvings before I saw them in the wild,” says Paul Nicklen, who keeps at home a soapstone carving of two brothers fighting over the first seal, the elder having stolen the younger one’s catch. “Such powerful, evocative, visceral storytelling,” he says, which taught him to see the world in shapes, colors and stories. As for Cristina, his diving and fieldwork partner, she sees differently: “She’s all about the empty spaces and I’m all about getting that animal to be in my face and be close.” A two-voice book is in the works, possibly called “Side by Side.” They are approaching 60, he reckons they have “15, 16 years left,” and they fully intend to enjoy them.

Reverence by Paul Nicklen is published by Hemeria (360 pages, from $124) in English and French editions. The photographer will sign copies at Paris Photo on Friday November 13, 2026, at 3 p.m., at the Hemeria booth (P19, Galerie Courbe Sud), Grand Palais, Paris.

"paragraph", "text": "在其他地方，阿尔瓦·巴拉苏布拉马尼亚姆（Alwar Balasubramaniam）的装置《Not Just for true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，兰贾尼·谢塔（Ranjani Shettar）的《Under the same sky》（2026）如植物华盖般在头顶展开。这些大型、苍白的植物形态带有淡淡的黄色，它们抽芽并绽放——完全由棉花和钢铁手工编织而成，随后上漆，每一片花瓣和卷须都是耐心、不紧不慢的劳动的结晶。它们的影子在地面上以一种安静的丰盈感延伸，既错综复杂又模糊不清。站在装置下方，人们感受到的不是悲伤，而是一种更温柔的东西：苦乐参半的记忆中那部分不会作痛的部分——一种安静的认知：有时，家是一个美丽而转瞬即逝的拥抱。", "paragraph", "text": "最终，你恍然大悟，关怀与失落其实是同一回事——它们系于同一个地方，却在时间的不同时刻被体验到。在你的内心深处，某个房间里仍然闪烁着一盏灯，而你已经多年未曾踏入。墙壁或许已经消失。地址或许已不再属于你。但站在那个门廊里、沐浴在金色午后余晖中的记忆，永远属于你，由你珍藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shreya Ajmani 是一位作家和艺术专业人士，专注于亚洲及其流散群体艺术。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Shows

Home Is a Fleeting Embrace: India at the 61st Venice Biennale

SUMAKSHI SINGH ’s

Permanent Address , 2026, at the India Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026. Photo by and copyright Joe Habben. Courtesy the India Pavilion.

Geographies of Distance: remembering home India Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale Arsenale di Venezia May 9–Nov 22, 2026

Light enters the vast Isolotto warehouse, filtered and curious. Wispy white, lace-like forms catch my eye first; I move toward them before I even mean to. Sumakshi Singh’s Permanent Address (2026) gradually comes into focus. The installation is a monumental, ghostly recreation of the home her grandparents moved into as refugees in New Delhi after the 1947 partition of India. “33 Link Road,” as the artist remembers, is where members of the family were birthed and married. Afternoons spent knitting and embroidering with her grandmother led to this threaded homage, where memory takes on its own afterlife.

The set-up of the India Pavilion recalls an abandoned plot with the kind of postcolonial-era bungalows I used to walk past as a child—houses still standing, but empty, with no heirs to return to them. The exhibition, titled “Geographies of Distance: remembering home” and curated by Amin Jaffer, imagines home as something assembled—pieced together from textures and rituals we repeat without quite noticing. Conceived as a surreal private dwelling, the room holds a faint layout of a house, a panorama of a town nearby, towering bamboo, dry soil, and bulbous flowering forms. To move through it is to walk through a memory forming before you.

Installation view of ASIM WAQIF ’s Chaal , 2026, at the India Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026. Photo by and copyright Joe Habben. Courtesy the India Pavilion.

ALWAR BALASUBRAMANIAM ’s

Not Just for Us , 2026, at the India Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026. Photo by and copyright Andrea Avezzù. Courtesy the India Pavilion.

Near Singh’s ethereal structure, the bamboos in Asim Waqif’s Chaal (2026) shoot upward and sideways—dense and unapologetically expansive. Where Singh’s home dissolves into thread, Waqif remains steadfast. It draws on the visual grammar of scaffolding that perpetually blankets cities across India: construction in permanent mid-sentence, always in a state of becoming. There is a rugged quality to Waqif’s edifice, as if it might outlast both the hands that built it.

Elsewhere, Alwar Balasubramaniam’s installation, Not Just for Us (2026), embodies an entirely different register. The sculptural panels are made of clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu, where he works, bearing cracks caused by the natural process of evaporation, which reify the passage of time and ecological fragility. Rather than metaphorizing home through mournful nostalgia, it presents the water cycle as a repetitive ritual of belonging and renewal. Yet the piece also captures the resilience of the land, and how it endures despite seasonal fluctuations.

SKARMA SONAM TASHI ’s

Echoes of Home , 2026, at the India Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026. Photo by and copyright Andrea Avezzù. Courtesy the India Pavilion.

Positioned against one wall, Skarma Sonam Tashi’s Echoes of Home (2026) resembles a mountain settlement. The structure comprises clusters of earth-colored blocks made from papier-mâché of cardboard and discarded books, which the artist soaked and bound with tamarind seed glue and clay from Leh, suggesting Ladakhi dwellings through outline and residue. Despite its seemingly compact architecture, the work feels deliberately fragile with its flimsy, impermanent materiality, standing in for a landscape, and way of life, that is itself in constant flux.

Meanwhile, Ranjani Shettar’s Under the same sky (2026) unfurls overhead like a vegetal awning. The large, pale botanical forms, tinged with deep yellow, sprout and blossom—entirely handwoven from cotton and steel, then lacquered, each petal and tendril is the result of patient, unhurried labor. Their shadows stretch across the floor in quiet abundance, at once intricate and indistinct. Standing beneath the installation, one does not feel grief, but something softer: that part of a bittersweet memory that does not ache—the quiet knowledge that, sometimes, home is a beautiful, fleeting embrace.

Installation views of RANJANI SHETTAR ’s Under the same sky , 2026, at the India Pavilion, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026. Photo by and copyright Andrea Avezzù. Courtesy the India Pavilion.

Taken together, “Geographies of Distance: remembering home” does what only the most careful acts of remembrance can: it holds the ungraspable without fully clutching it. The presentation does not elegize what was once home so much as locate its remnants in unlikely, often overlooked places. Memories of the past are attached not only to physical addresses, but to the smaller, more ordinary textures: hallways that now only exist as delicate maps in your mind; the particular feeling of a space that you once lived in and tended to.

Eventually, it dawns on you that care and loss are the same thing—tied to the same place, but experienced at different moments in time. Somewhere within you, a light still flickers in a room you have not entered in years. The walls may be gone. The address may no longer belong to you. But the memory of standing in that doorway, basking in the glow of that golden afternoon, is always yours to keep.

Shreya Ajmani is a writer and art professional focusing on art from Asia and its diasporas.

They have also amplified her appreciation of the rights and freedoms she now enjoys as a citizen of Australia, where she migrated in 2007, then as a lapsed photojournalist and emerging artist. “I grew up under a system that didn’t give me freedom of speech, or equal rights as a woman, so I don’t take it for granted,” she says."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6adad47b9a5c5453be36d01d5365362970b260a5/0_0_4826_7239/master/4826.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Artist Hoda Afshar stands against a brick wall, pulling down a large black cloth", "caption": "Hoda Afshar: ‘Iran’s struggles and our movements are often hijacked and used for other political purposes and ends.’ Photograph: Adam Ferguson/The Guardian", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But it has also made her more sensitive to Australia’s human rights and social justice failures: “Australia claims beautiful values. It is the country of a ‘fair go’, that wants everything equal for everybody. But rights are not distributed equally.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“From the beginning, I was very excited to be able to critique authority; to be a responsible citizen in a society where we can fight for change,” she adds."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This combination of lived experience and strongly held values has resulted in some of the most vivid, urgent and achingly beautiful works of Australian art seen in the last decade – several of which are brought together in a/part, her new exhibition at the University of Melbourne’s Buxton Contemporary", "links": [{"text": "Australian art", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/australian-art"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The show brings together three projects that deal with what she calls “states of exception”, a term coined by the Italian political theorist Giorgio Agamben for “sites where the laws that are applied to normal citizens don’t apply or can be broken,” Afshar says."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a5ded8c46f7e2b92472600286a4915e8d1527995/0_0_2500_1567/master/2500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Photo of gallery installation of Hoda Afshar’s portrait photographs, with each subject obscuring their face", "caption": "Afshar’s Code Black/Riot on display at Buxton Contemporary, the University of Melbourne. Almost a decade later, it is her most exhibited work in Australia and abroad."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9de00d73f87f83dfc55877c88aec3db4e14ce9a0/0_0_1920_1080/master/1920.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Two men embrace on a sandy beach, waves lapping nearby, from the video Remain", "caption": "A still from Remain, 2018. article_text:
W hen Hoda Afshar was a teenager, coming of age in theocratic and authoritarian Iran in the 1990s, she and her friends were repeatedly arrested and physically punished by the “morality police”, for wearing their hijabs incorrectly in public and for attending underground parties. “They used to put a few of us in small solitary confinement cells together for a night or two, it was very common for my generation to experience that,” she says.

“We are part of the nasl-e sukhteh , or ‘burned generation’; the generation born after the 1979 revolution, who had to pay the price for many of the transformations and changes that happened.”

These formative experiences left the artist with an ongoing sensitivity to injustice, and an interest in incarceration, marginalisation and state violence. They have also amplified her appreciation of the rights and freedoms she now enjoys as a citizen of Australia, where she migrated in 2007, then as a lapsed photojournalist and emerging artist. “I grew up under a system that didn’t give me freedom of speech, or equal rights as a woman, so I don’t take it for granted,” she says.

But it has also made her more sensitive to Australia’s human rights and social justice failures: “Australia claims beautiful values. It is the country of a ‘fair go’, that wants everything equal for everybody. But rights are not distributed equally.”

“From the beginning, I was very excited to be able to critique authority; to be a responsible citizen in a society where we can fight for change,” she adds.

This combination of lived experience and strongly held values has resulted in some of the most vivid, urgent and achingly beautiful works of Australian art seen in the last decade – several of which are brought together in a/part, her new exhibition at the University of Melbourne’s Buxton Contemporary

The show brings together three projects that deal with what she calls “states of exception”, a term coined by the Italian political theorist Giorgio Agamben for “sites where the laws that are applied to normal citizens don’t apply or can be broken,” Afshar says.

For each project, she has created video and photographic portraits that foreground the humanity of her subjects, while interrogating the narratives that underpin each state of exception; the ways of depicting a marginalised person or group that make it possible to accept their disenfranchisement.

Best known among these works is Remain , the 2018 work Afshar made with the Kurdish Iranian journalist and author Behrouz Boochani and a group of refugee men detained on Manus Island as part of Australia’s offshore immigration detention system. Shot on a tiny island near Manus, the two-channel video marries the beguilingly beautiful aesthetic of the tropical paradise with poetry, Kurdish song and personal testimony to express the humanity of its subjects – and the depth of their suffering.

“The intention was to create a new visual language that can impact people about this issue, because we have become absolutely immune to images of suffering from the refugee crisis,” Afshar told me back when Remain debuted in 2018. Almost a decade later, it is her most exhibited work in Australia and abroad.

Code Black/Riot, showing at Buxton for the first time since its debut at the Sydney Biennale in March, is an immersive video installation and series of portraits focusing on Indigenous youth in detention shot in far north Queensland.

after newsletter promotion

Created with Boochani and Kuku Yalandji/Waanji/Yidinji/Gugu Yimithirr artist Vernon Ah Kee, the video features former detainees and staff from a youth detention centre, talking about living and working within a dehumanising system.

The former staff talk about the rainbow-coloured system of “codes” used to identify security and safety issues, and the practice of “night mode”, in which children are locked in their cells, in pitch dark, for days at a time. The children describe beatings from guards, solitary confinement, and a seemingly endless cycle of arrests, incarceration and probation.

To protect the identities of her young subjects, Afshar shot them in tight closeup, focusing on bodies and the lower halves of faces, highlighting the tension in the children’s bodies and mouths as they share harrowing experiences.

The studio-based interviews are intercut with footage of the young people: navigating Cairns at night amid revelling locals and tourists, floating in rivers and waterholes, perching in trees and bouncing on trampolines.

“It was very important not to depict them as broken,” Afshar says of the children; their photographic portraits show them in playful and defiant poses, using hands, flowers, face paint and clothing to obscure their faces.

As in Remain, beauty is juxtaposed with violence; the humanity of the narrators is contrasted with the inhumanity of the systems they are trapped in.

Her 2021 project Agonistes , spotlighting prominent Australian whistleblowers such as the former Australian army lawyer David McBride , explores a different “state of exception”: government employees who breach confidentiality agreements to speak up about witnessing wrongdoing, and are prosecuted and imprisoned as a result.

“These people all made a sacrifice; they had to choose between the law and the public, and they chose the public, believing that if the public knows what is happening, things will change,” says Afshar. “They lose everything because they believe in the values that the society claims to have.”

A fourth work, Shafaq, premiering in a/part, is more personal. Made during a camping trip on Larrakia country in the Northern Territory in July, it reflects her anxiety as the US resumed bombing Iran’s south, where her family lives. Shafaq is “a conversation across distance to my family members”, she says.

The last year has been difficult, with career highs marred by grief and anxiety over the bombing of her homeland. “Seeing places that you grew up in being demolished like that, it’s like part of your body and identity is being erased by it too. It’s a kind of pain I didn’t know till that moment,” she says.

The way Iran has been portrayed internationally has left her sceptical of documentary modes of storytelling. “Our struggles and our movements are often hijacked and used for other political purposes and ends,” she says. “I wanted to rethink what documentary means, to allow for interpretation; to never present an image with concrete messaging or didacticism.”

The end goal of her art, she says, is to bring people together. “For me, it’s not about east or west, right or left, or these binaries that keep us endlessly separated and fighting with each other. I don’t belong to anyone’s camps … What I care about is human life and human dignity.”

Hoda Afshar’s a/part is on at Buxton Contemporary, the University of Melbourne, until 24 April 2027. Entry is free

article_text:
Friedel Dzubas spent most of his career making enormous, vibrant Color Field–esque abstract paintings. But for a brief stint in the early 1960s, he abandoned color altogether. He became so taken with the outcome of that period—a series of soft yet stark black-and-white paintings—that he dreamed of finding a Baroque chapel somewhere in Europe and covering its walls with them.

He never got his chapel. But more than 30 years after his death, the German-born painter has come surprisingly close.

On opening night of “ Friedel Dzubas: Darkness into Light” at the exhibition space shared by Nathalie Karg Gallery and Jules Lazare in Manhattan, Robert Keith, a director at the gallery, walked me through a room filled with the artist’s rarely seen black-and-white paintings. Keith pointed out that the building was once a school belonging to the neighboring Ukrainian church. Dzubas, he said, would have been enormously proud to see his work displayed there. It was something he’d wanted all his life.

“If Dzubas sees us from above, I’m sure he’s very happy,” Karg told me a few days later during a chat on the second floor of the gallery.

The exhibition, organized with Nicolas Graille of the gallery Jules Lazare, revisits one of the strangest and most personal periods in the career of an artist who knew just about everybody in the New York art world but never became quite as famous as many of his friends.

Dzubas was born in Berlin in 1915 to a Catholic mother and a Jewish father. He fled Nazi Germany for the United States in 1939 and eventually found himself among the painters who would change American art. He knew Jackson Pollock , shared a studio with Helen Frankenthaler , and became friends with the influential critic Clement Greenberg. He participated in the famous Ninth Street Show in 1951 and had a solo exhibition at Leo Castelli’s gallery in 1958. In other words, he was hardly an outsider. He was there when Abstract Expressionism was becoming the dominant force in American painting.

Yet Dzubas could never outrun the enormous shadow of his better-known contemporaries. Yes, his pictures found their way into major museums, including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Guggenheim, and he had a retrospective at the Hirshhorn Museum in Washington, D.C., in 1983. But his name doesn’t carry anything like the recognition of Pollock or Frankenthaler.

Why not? Karg thinks the answer may be as simple as changing tastes. “It’s fashion, it’s taste, it’s the generations that change,” she said. Sometimes an artist enjoys enormous success, only to fall out of favor as collectors move on. Sometimes an artist’s moment arrives much later.

Dzubas’s black paintings are a prime example of this phenomenon.

In 1959, after finally becoming an American citizen, the artist returned to Germany for the first time in 20 years. It was an emotionally complicated homecoming. In the late 1930s he escaped a country that was descending into Nazism, leaving his family behind. According to Graille, who has worked closely with the artist’s daughter and estate, surviving letters from Dzubas’s mother suggest she was deeply hurt by his departure and long absence. “You left, you abandoned us,” Graille recalled her writing in one of her letters to Dzubas.

Exactly what happened during that visit is impossible to reconstruct. Dzubas traveled through Germany and Austria, visiting Baroque churches and spending time at a monastery. The trip seems to have awakened his interest in the Catholic traditions of his childhood, along with memories of the country he’d left behind. “He was always, at his core, I think, still a traditional European painter,” Graille said.

Soon afterward, Dzubas began making paintings that looked almost nothing like the colorful abstractions associated with his name.

The bright, expansive shapes had disappeared. In their place came black marks, gray washes, looping lines, and dense arrangements of brushstrokes somewhere between Twombly’s chalk drawings and Pollock’s contained chaos. Some look almost like handwriting, though there’s nothing to read. Others suggest crosses, figures, or religious scenes. Several have borders worked into the composition that hint at the ornate frames associated with Old Master works or religious paintings, giving them the appearance of devotional objects.

The titles offer clues of what Dzubas was thinking: Temptation , Betrayal , Rex , and Walpurgis , the last a reference to a German festival with pagan roots.

The works were shown at Robert Elkon Gallery in 1962, where the critical response was mixed. In the New York Times , Brian O’Doherty wrote that the works appeared gloomy and largely unconvincing. Donald Judd, who back then was a young critic and artist, was more impressed, even if his praise was charmingly restrained. “This one is not bad,” Judd wrote, after dismissing Dzubas’s previous two exhibitions.

The paintings didn’t find much of a market, either. Dzubas soon returned to color, and the black works largely disappeared from view. Karg thinks the timing was unfortunate. By the early ’60s, the art world was falling in love with Pop art. Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein were offering collectors bright colors, recognizable images, and a decidedly different mood. Dzubas, meanwhile, was painting pictures that were, as Karg put it, “sinister.” Not exactly what collectors at the time were looking for.

Graille believes these paintings could be the most revealing works Dzubas ever made, bringing together his German upbringing, American career, religious interests, and complicated family history. “To me, this body of work is probably the most overlooked of his whole career, and the most original, most personal work that he made,” he said.

Graille first became involved with Dzubas’s work nearly a decade ago, when he met the artist’s daughter, Hanni. He later began working with the estate, which had continued to find buyers for Dzubas’s better-known paintings of the ’60s and ’70s. The black works, however, had received little attention.

When Graille and Karg met through a mutual friend, they realized their interests complemented one another. Karg had been increasingly interested in revisiting historical artists, while Graille was working with estates and establishing his own gallery, Jules Lazare, which he named in tribute to his late mother.

The two remain separate businesses but share some expenses and collaborate on exhibitions. Next month they’ll open a show of work by Larry Poons. For Karg, the partnership provides an opportunity to look beyond the younger artists who dominate so much of the contemporary gallery business.

“There are so many good artists, but they have never been really accounted for,” she said.

And collectors are beginning to pay attention to Dzubas again. According to data from ARTDAI, the artist’s annual auction sales have grown considerably over the past decade, from $468,226 across 14 lots offered in 2016 to more than $1.6 million across 25 lots offered in 2025. In May, his painting Entrance , offered alongside another work, sold at Christie’s for $160,000, against a high estimate of $100,000. ( All figures are hammer prices. )

The market hasn’t been entirely immune to the broader slowdown. Dzubas’s sell-through rate has slipped to 81.3 percent so far in 2026, with 3 of 16 lots failing to find buyers.

Still, when I asked Graille about the market, he seemed almost offended by the premise. “The market is great, but who cares?” he said. “Art is about more than sales.” He’s also encouraged by renewed institutional interest. Graille said that German collector Reinhard Ernst, whose museum in Wiesbaden holds a major collection of Frankenthaler’s work, has been assembling what he described as the world’s largest collection of Dzubas paintings. Ernst now owns 12 works from the black series, some of which are on loan to the New York exhibition. The museum is planning a Dzubas retrospective for June 2027.

The New York show has found buyers, too. Karg said several paintings had sold, with others on reserve. Graille described the exhibition as nearly sold out, with particular interest in the larger works. For paintings that struggled to find buyers in 1962, that’s quite a turnaround.

But the more interesting question may be what this renewed attention means for Dzubas’s reputation. His colorful paintings have for years secured his place in the history of postwar American abstraction. The black series suggests there’s another, more complicated story to tell. And that brings the artist back to the church.

In a 1982 interview, Dzubas described becoming obsessed with the possibility of filling a chapel with his black drawings. He imagined them covering the architecture, turning the space into something between an exhibition and a religious experience. He died in 1994, never having realized the project.

Now, in a former church school on Manhattan’s Lower East Side, some of those paintings have finally found a home that would have made sense to him. It isn’t the Baroque chapel he imagined, but it’s probably the next best thing.

article_text:
In the Cairo-based gallery’s latest exhibition, six artists use textiles to examine the limits and possibilities in acts of repair.

With a brief and rather cryptic exhibition statement, Gypsum’s latest group show, The Mountain Cannot Repair Itself , showcases the work of gallery-represented artists alongside young and emerging artists who are not (yet) affiliated with it. The exhibition’s focus on textiles is alluded to briskly in the statement and then the works of each participating artist is summarised and explained. The exhibition title already brings to mind the possibility and impossibility of the act of mending, with the idea that ‘stitching’ is not only an act of repair but also of bringing disparate parts together. This latter metaphor perhaps encapsulates the works in the exhibition.

The exhibited works, by a total of six artists, cluster around notions of received memory and the traces that linger, expressed specifically through textiles, whether linens, tablecloths (in the work of Gözde İlkin and Layla Tag), handwoven tableaux (Marianne Fahmy) or elaborate constructions and the marking of space (Aisha Azab and Omar Abd Elbaqi). I struggled to place the work of Rawan Abbas in this constellation. Her fabric tableau and soft sculpture seemed to reference something specific to the artist and her practice, but not immediately perceptible to an audience in the context of this particular exhibition.

Perhaps the most visually captivating work is that of Layla Tag. The subtle elaborate constructions, in the series WHY DO PEOPLE DREAM? (2024), HOW DID YOU KNOW WHEN TO STOP? (2026) and Wonderfully Damaged (2024), project a significant sense of fragility with their flesh tones and watercoloured abstracted human/floral figures, underscored by a hint of macabre eroticism. There is the feeling of being exposed to something intensely private, and yet the scale, sense of colour and intricate stitching bring back the idea of mending or bringing together experiences and realities that are difficult to integrate.

This dimension is somehow mirrored in İlkin’s appliqué piece, Zeytin | Olive (2019), with its collected fabrics and textile tokens that look markedly personal but which also give an unmitigated sense of warm domesticity. Parts of the fabric, which are taken from tablecloths (and other household items), will immediately remind the viewer of their own childhood and family home. The soft human forms that she weaves against and on top of these fabrics reinforces a sense of intimacy and softness that is both delicate and beautiful.

Certain works bear resemblance and affinity to others. Abd Elbaqi’s Panoptic (2021) echoes some of the work of Shady El Noshokaty (specifically his work Latitude , part of the project Colony , which was exhibited at Gypsum in 2015) and also of Rodeina Fouad, They Fossilized Us (2023–25) and Tapestry of Self (2023). Abd Elbaqi’s more subtle mapping of certain urban elements of the Sayeda Zeinab district in Cairo, on sheer organza, gives a sense of fragility but also of an elusive transparency. Something that is seen and unseen. The stitching of urban forms that look like hybrids on sheer fabric raises the question of their possible survival and visibility.

A more private and yet impersonal kind of mapping is Azab’s small-scale abstract, layered mappings in The mountain can’t repair itself (2026). It is a painstaking mapping of a certain geography that is analytical but purposefully private, with what look like secret coded guides to an unknown place. There is a certain interiority to the work, akin to that of Tag’s, but Azab’s piece is visibly more abstract.

In all of these pieces there is a particular interiority and play with hybridity and form that is at the opposite end of Fahmy’s work. The two large-scale tableaux mimic vintage cartes postales of Alexandria and bring to mind the notion of not only bygone memories but also fantastical future projections of what might become of the past. There is a lightness and space in Fahmy’s embroideries that is a welcome change from the compact intensity of some of the other textiles. Not that her work is less intricate or meticulous, but its stitching technique gives a certain abstracted form of space that suits the speculative element in it. What kind of future can we imagine from a certain point in the past?

There is something to ponder about the mountain as a fault line or as the point where tectonic plates meet, collide or slide against each other and distort the earth’s surface to create different varieties of geological formations. Mountains will eventually wither away, although not at any scale of time that is intelligible to humans. The question lingers, what can we do to repair a fantastic distortion? Perhaps this can be achieved through the simple act of mending, as subtle and meticulous as the works in this exhibition.

The Mountain Cannot Repair Itself runs until 31 October

article_text:
葛藤を越えて日本で花開いた「Neo Pin-Up」

東京・神保町の New Gallery で、インドネシア出身のアーティスト・Ferdi（フェル）による個展 「Neo Pin-Up: Tokyo」 が10月23日から11月1日まで開催される。 本展でFerdiが発表するのは、日本のミニマルなイラストと、インドネシアの伝統的な染め物であるバティックの緻密な模様を組み合わせた新作。簡潔な線やかたちと豊かな装飾が響き合う画面には、キャラクターの魅力とともにふたつの文化が交わる独自の世界が広がっている。日本と母国の双方に向けられた作家の眼差しを通して、現代の視覚文化におけるピンナップの可能性に触れられる展覧会だ。

展覧会タイトルにも冠された「Neo Pin-Up」の背景には、作家自身が長く抱えてきた葛藤がある。1990年代のインドネシアでマンガや映画のポスターに親しみ、ピンナップに惹かれたFerdiは、保守的な価値観が根強い母国でこうした妖艶な描写が修正される場面を目にするうちに、好きなジャンルを描くことにためらいを抱えるようになる。一度、ピンナップから距離を置き、シンガポールでデザインを学んだFerdiにとって、転機となったのは2020年の日本留学。日本では世代を問わずピンナップを楽しんでいる様子を見たFerdiは、描くことへの情熱を取り戻す。そして2023年、クラシックな様式を現代的に再解釈するシリーズを始動させた。シリーズに込めた想いについて、作家は次のように語っている。

「私にとって、ピンナップは単に肌を露出したり、あからさまに過激に描いたりすることとはまったくの別物です。このシリーズは、ピンナップアートの本当の魅力は、人の身体が持つしなやかなシルエット、その場に流れる空気感、そして温度や香りまで伝わってくるようなさりげない雰囲気のなかにこそある、という想いのもとに描かれています」

現代のシンプルさと伝統の細密さを重ねて

新作のなかでFerdiが試みているのは、自身の作品にもっとも大きな影響を与えてきた日本のイラストとより深くつながることである。同時に、母国インドネシアが育んできたバティックの文様を画面に取り入れることで、伝統文化への敬意も表している。現代的なシンプルさと伝統的な細密さという対照的な要素を1枚の絵のなかで共存させる手法は、身体のシルエットや装飾、余白の関係を探ってきたFerdiならではのアプローチといえるだろう。インドネシア、シンガポールと日本で培ってきた感性が新作でどのような実を結んだのか、会場で確かめてほしい。
